[Taylor, Tom];[Coyne, Joseph Stirling] The Vicar of Wakefield An Original Drama in three acts 60 pp (UW copy)
J. Stirling Coyne is listed as the author of a play of this title on the title-page of his play "My Wife's Daughter" also in this Volume. However, in Volume 1, the anonymous play, "The Philosopher's Stone" is attributed to the author of "The Vicar of Wakefield" and "Diogenes", whilst "Diogenes" (Volume 1) is attributed to the author of "Parents and Guardians". This latter is known to be by Tom Taylor, and Nicoll lists Taylor as the author also of "The Vicar of Wakefield". It is plausible that this play was co-authored by Taylor and Stirling Coyne, although they are not known to have collaborated on anything else. "Sir Roger de Coverley" (Taylor) (Volume 4) is also listed as being by the author of "Diogenes", "The Vicar of Wakefield", "The Philosopher's Stone", and "Prince Dorus". body.head: The Vicar of Wakefield.

div.stage: Scene I.—A hayfield—In the distance L. Squire Thornhill's mansion, embowered in wood, the spire of the village church R. —More in the foreground (c.) the white cottage of Dr. Primrose —The hawthorn and honeysuckle bank ground piece across the stage at back, with stile in centre—a stone back and front, for steps—A rustic table and seats U. E. R. H . — The Curtain rises to pastoral music—Sheep-bells and the chirupping of birds in the distance.
Enter Ephraim Jenkinson, U. C. R. H., with a whip, cautiously, and looking off; he crosses the stile, and comes down c.

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: There, I've marked down the covey—old cock, old hen, and cheepers (taking letter from pocket). Here's a note, now, for that pretty bit of plumpness, Miss Livy. She's for the Squire's own eating; but, hang me, if I don't have the picking of the old bird, and that very young cock, Master Moses, myself. I could pity the girl, poor thing ! Scarce settled in the nest a week, and already (sighs). Hey! what's this, Ephraim Jenkinson? Snivelling? Ah! this comes of doing the devil's work on commission. Once let me get this rakehelly Squire Thornhill's job off my hands and I'll forswear all roguery on anybody's account but my own. Sola! (Looks off L. H.) Petticoats! Oh! two of the Squire's ladies of quality, and old friends of my own, on the same devil's errand as myself. A pair of decoy ducks, to tempt the poor little widgeon yonder into the net; and then — Oh you Jezabels! (Retires up c.)

div.stage: Enter Lady Blarney and Miss Wilhelmina Skeggs fanning themselves 1. E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: (L.) Ho! this 'orrid 'ot weather.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: (R.) And nothink but these nasty green fields to walk in—no Ranelagh!

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: No Mall! no tea-houses!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: No Gray's Inn Gardings, with spruce templars to ogle.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: How I 'ate lambs, and 'aycocks, and hinnocence, and all that 'ere !

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: But, where's this pretty lambkin of a shepherdess, that the Squire's run wild after?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Some awkward wretch, I'll warrant, with cheeks—

sp.speaker: Jenkins
sp.p: (Coming down c.) Of the fickle country-red that comes and goes, not the London fast colour—eh ladies?. (pointing to their faces.)

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: (L.) Paint, indeed? (drawing up) I scorn the insinuation. Address yourself to your ekals, fellow.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: (R.) (Drawing up.) And not to persons of quality!

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Quality? there's good and bad qualities, d'ye see, Molly? (Whispers in her ear.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: (Screams.) Ah ! Why, how the dickens?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: (Alarmed.) Eh?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Oh! don't be alarmed, Jenny. (Whispers in her ear.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.|Lady B.
sp.p: Why it's—

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: (Changing his manner ) "Captain Starlight, of the great North Road," my Bona Robas; or "Dimber Jemmy of the Mint"—if you like that better; or, "Ned of the Fambles," well known at St. Giles's Round-house,the hemp-blocks in Bridewell, the cart's tail, and other places of public amusement. I've as many trades as aliases, and as many faces as names. This is my honest face,—no wonder you did not know it.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Why, my gallant captain!

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Give as your hand, my bold boy! (Shakes hands.) To think of meeting a town acquaintance in this 'orrid, low, uncultivated 'ayfield.

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Why, I'm recommended country air, for a sort of tickling in the throat, which London does not agree with just now—hem! especially about Bow-street. So as my friend, Squire Thornhill, wanted a little assistance here (pointing over his shoulder at cottage) in the old way—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Have you seen her ?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: I've been watching her at romps in the hayfield, with her brothers and sisters this half-hour—and be hanged to me (aside) Yonder they are. (Retiring up, and looking L. H.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Poor thing! but care killed a cat. I see we are on the same lay.

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Excuse me, my business is to tempt her to the edge of the pit; you have the more delicate task of pushing her in. I've a letter for her here, if she'll take it, and then—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Ah! the old plan! Honest Frank, the Squire's chaplain, was to have introduced us this morning; but he rather overdid the claret last night—which is she?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: (Pointing off L.) There, that dark-haired one, who has just tumbled her venerable papa over the haycock.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: 'Ow 'orrid ungenteel!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Shall we join 'em, Capting?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Why, I'm not exactly the figure to attend ladies of quality, and, then, I must plant my lime twig alone (shewing letter), or good bye to the Squire's little black bird, and my little goldfinches. (Slapping his pocket and crosses to L.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Ah! the Squire does pay 'ansum.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Quite the man of honour, every inch of 'im!

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: (L.) Eh? as I live, here comes old Flamborough. (Looking L. 2 E., and runs R. H.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: A friend of yours?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: I sold him a horse last week.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: For a few shiners more than he was worth? Eh, Capting?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Au contraire, for half his value—pon honour— you see I got him cheap. ( Winks.)

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: But why run away, if you sold the horse a bargain ?

sp.speaker: Jenkins.
sp.p: Why the awkward fact is, I had a fit of remorse, and stole him back again yesterday.

div.stage: Exit Jenkinson 1 E. R. H.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, as the Capting has an engagement, we can't introduce ourselves. I should sink into my shoe 'eels.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: No, its only your real high-bred ones that 'as your genuine easy assurance. Best trapes back to the Squire's, and see if that fat 'edded parson 'ave slept off his wine yet.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And then we can drop in on the family here, in a degagee way with the Squire, in the cool of the evening. (Crosses to L.) So, come along, the Honourable Miss Wilhelmina Carolina Amelia Skeggsl

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: After you, the Right Honourable the Lady Blarney ! Ha! ha!

div.stage: Exit Miss S. and Lady B. 1 E. L. H.
Enter Burchell followed by Dame and Farmer Flamborough, 2 E. L. H.—Burchell seats himself on the stile— The Dame crosses to R.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: (L.) Yes, its a zight too bad, Master Burchell, look, ye. Three weeks it is you're had our best chamber, and never a varden 'ave we touched of your coin.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Oh! (Whistling, and switching off the heads of the nettles with his stick.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: (R.) Noa, Varmer's right, never a varden 'are we touched of your coin.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Wilt hold thy chatterin' tongue, Dame? What's to be done wi' un?

sp.speaker: Dame
sp.p: All! What's to be done wi' un?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Now, why can't you do as I do?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: How's that say'ee?

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Ah! How's that, say'ee?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: You can't get any money, no more can I. I'm patient, why aren't you?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Ecod, he'd anger a saint, Dame!

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Let alone thee and me, Varmer.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Wilt hold thy clapper, I say?—and he's a zittin there as cool as a dairy pan, and a whistlin, and a zwitchin, and a zmilin, as sweet as the stone babes a top of the Thornhill tomb.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: I've told you an unnecessary number of times, my good Farmer, that I've no money.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: What? Ecod! What do'st say to that, Dame? (Scratching his head.)

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: No money?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: And to see thee flinging half-crowns away, like potato-peelings, on gypsies, and beggars, and vagabonds.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Ah!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: And a keeping thy lawful landlord and landlady out of their own.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: It's zinful. (Loud.)

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: It's scandalous. (Loud.)

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Tis abominable (Louder.)

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: 'Tis—what's the Vicar's word?—'tis deuterogamous!

div.stage: Enter Dr. Primrose, U. E. L. H.—Burchell rises, and lifts his hat as he gets over the stile.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (c.) Holloa! Holloa! brawling in the church—Eh?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: (L.) The church, your Reverence!

sp.speaker: Dame
sp.p: (R.) The church, your Reverence!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Yes, church. This field, with its sweet air, its wild flowers, and its summer stillness, what is it, but a temple of the Great Being (lifts his hat) wherein strife, and anger, and evil speaking, are a sin and a profanation?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: (Respectfully.) I ask your pardon, your Reverence. I did not think—

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: How can you, when your'e always talking?

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: (Aside.) Ecod, his Reverence had Varmer there!

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (R. C.) You should lecture me, for the sin lies at my door. The fact is, I owe these honest people a couple of guineas, and I can't pay them.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: And a gave three guineas, yesterday was two days, to the beadle to spare the broken old soldier they'd ha' whipped through the village for dog stealing. (Farmer and Dame retire up and converse at back.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p:
Extravagant youth. (Aside.) Noble fellow! I love him. In future, young man, be just before you are generous; and, now, allow me to lend you what you owe this worthy
couple. (Taking a couple of guineas from his pocket, and giving them to Burchell.)

sp.speaker: Burchell.
sp.p: (R. C.) I take it, with all my heart, Sir (bluntly); and I am glad of my imprudence, as it shows me there are still men like you in the world—but, I fear, I may inconvenience you.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, 'tis true I have just exchanged affluence for poverty; but, what then—I am not so poor, but that I have a spare guinea or two for the occasion.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: You seem to take the fall from wealth to want, like a philosopher.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Sir, I have those supports which philosophers are often without, trust in a Higher Being, and the will to do my duty. I am blessed with sound health, a notable wife, a good and loving family; and I mean to allow of no wants in my parish, but three.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: And they?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Are strange wants. A parson wanting pride, young men wanting wives, and alehouses wanting customers. You see, I am frank with you, Sir. In return, tell me something of yourself.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: I have little to tell, Sir; except that I am a sort of well-read, well-bred vagabond; too proud to beg, too lazy to work, and who asks no more than to saunter carelessly through life, and play with the children—the only human beings I have found to be harmless. Still, I can honour learning, charity, and humility when I find them, as I did in your last Sunday's sermon.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ah! then you heard me in support of that great man, Dr. Whistom? You were with me there, Sir, I hope? (Dame and Farmer come down L. H.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, the sermons I prefer are those preached out of the pulpit, like yours just now, by good example. (crosses to L.) Here, Farmer (pays Flamborough), and now, I suppose, I may come back to play with the children, and be stormed at by you, as soon as I please.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: (L.) That thee may, Master Burchell, and much good may it do'ee. (Burchell crosses at back to R. H.)

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: (L.) Good day to your Reverence.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: (Makes a formal obeisance.) Good day to your Reverence.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Come, Dame! Is the 'oman going to stand like a cherry-clack, clatter, clatter, all day, with a wanion to thee? (Turns Dame round to L.) Drat thee! Wosbird, Wilt come, I say.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (R.) And remember, Farmer, no scolding.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: There, Dame, thee hears ! no scolding!

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Well I bean't a scolding!

div.stage: Exeunt Farmer and Dame scolding, 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (Crossing to L.)' Advice is like physic; everybody is glad to recommend to his neighbour, what he hates swallowing himself—but you're a stranger here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (R.) Stranger? hum. It's my rule to be at home everywhere, and at home nowhere, so I hardly know how to answer; but I've been familiar with this neighbourhood since I was a boy.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And I was going to be very wise, and tell you all about the place, though we only came hither last week; but you must be my guide instead. What think you of our Squire, Mr. Thornhill?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Why, that he ought to be much obliged to his uncle, Sir William, who leaves his nephew a fine house and five-sixths of his income, and lives himself on the other sixth, up two pair of stairs in London.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: They tell me, Sir William, is one of the best, and most generous men living.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (Pleased, but with an affectation of surliness.) Do they? Hum!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But whimsical.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Do they?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Some say absurd.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (Annoyed.) Do they?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Some go as far as to say, a perfect fool!

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: No, d—n it, not a fool.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Do you know him ?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: I know his history pretty well. In his youth he loved all mankind—for fortune prevented him from knowing that there were rascals. He relieved all who asked ; and found numbers disposed to solicit. His profusion gradually impaired his fortune; till,on the verge of ruin, he found that a man must give, not benefits alone; but his own heart, if he wished to gain the hearts of others. So he resolved to respect himself, and restore his shattered fortune. He travelled over Europe on foot; and, now, though he is scarce thirty, he is richer than ever; not quite such a fool as before—but still a greater fool than he is willing the world should take him for.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Young man, you've a smart gift of sketching character, I wish Moses had heard you;—you see the lad yonder— a young philosopher, Sir, reading Epictetus among the haycocks. He shall conduct you an argument in mood and figure, or draw you a parallel after the manner of Plutarch, as well as many an Oxford master. He is my pupil, Sir, and I am proud of him.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: I am afraid his light will be rather under a bushel here. (Laughter heard outside L. H. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And there are my girls, bless 'em, Olivia and Sophia— romantic names, but I protest I had no hand in 'em. I tried for Grizel, after their aunt; but their mother would not let me. But my Deborah must introduce them, for here she comes, with a bottle of our famous old gooseberry, and a rustic treat from our orchard, "dapes inemptas," as Horace hath it. You must stay and partake, Sir.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Primrose, 2 E. L. H., with a bottle of wine and a table-cloth—Burchell takes the bottle and places it on table R. H.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (c. Making a ceremonious curtsey.) I thank you, Sir, for your well-bred attention.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (L.) My dear, let me present to you, Mr.— Mr.—

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Burchell; at present a lodger with Farmer Flamborough, and no stranger to the notable qualities of Mrs. Primrose.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Sir, your most obedient. (Aside.) To have to lay the cloth before a strange gentleman!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Come, dame—bustle, bustle.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Allow me to assist you. (Taking cloth and spreading it on table R. H.) Madam; laying a cloth is one of the few things I do to my own satisfaction.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I hope he is not a footman out of place. (Aside.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: And catting whistles is another.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Sir! (In astonishment.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: And trying the merits of Mrs. Primrose's famous old gooseberry, will be a third, if she will invite me.

div.stage: Enter Farm Servant, U. E. L. H. over stile, with a basket of wine and corkscrew, glasses, fruits, &c., which he lays out on table—Burchell assisting.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (c.) Sir you are vastly polite, and kindly welcome. In the summer time, Sir, the Doctor likes these little entertainments under the honeysuckle, better than your formal luncheons, with their vulgar loads of meat—they suit his simple tastes.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (L.) Fiddle-de-dee, dame—they suit his empty pockets.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (Aside to the Doctor.) My dear! how can you let down the dignity of the family ?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Never mind the dignity of the family, just now, my dear; but think of their appetites. I'll give them the signal for dinner, the rogues, (Waves his handkerchief 2 E. L. H.) Aha! a race between Livy and Sophy!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And we shall have them coming up all blown about and blowsy, as rough as colts, and with faces as red as peonys.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (L. Looking off) Well footed, Livy, she's cleared the bridge. Sophy follows! take care, girl, you'll be down. Ha! —she slips on the plank!—she falls! The black pool! She sinks! Oh, heavens ! (Covers his face with his hands.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (L. E. Wringing her hands.) Oh ! run, run.

div.stage: Burchell ( R . ) rushes off 2. B. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (Gazes eagerly off and follows the actions of Burchell) Oh! Well done!—well done! The white dress!— he plunges. My child!—my child! (falls on his knees.) Thank God !-she's saved! Thank God !

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And, now, I'll faint.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Don't be a fool, woman. (Rises.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: If you have no feelings of your own, Doctor, respect mine. I insist upon fainting.

div.stage: Enter Olivia running, 2 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: (c.) She's quite safe! She's not hurt at all! Oh, my dear father! I scarce know whether to laugh or to cry. When Mr. Burchell jumped in splash, like old Diver, the water spaniel, I'm sure I should have laughed if it had been any one but our poor Sophy, floating down the stream; and to see him come up, puffing for breath! And so now Sophy's gone to put on some dry things; and I'll run after her, for I only stayed to tell you not to be frightened. I told Mr. Burchell we could lend one of Moses' old coats, if he did not mind looking funny.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But you'll ask Mr. Burchell to return and taste our country fare here?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: ( C ) Yes, Papa.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (R.) And you, Livy, come back when you've put Sophy to bed and given her a dish of tansey tea.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, please! she doesn't want to go to bed, and she hates tansey tea, and she has such an appetite for dinner —at least, I have, and it's all the same;—so, if we might both come back—do, Papa!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Agreed—agreed! Come, Dame, spare her the tansey tea—we'll give them ten minutes to change, and then —hey for gratitude and gooseberry!

div.stage: Exit Olivia 2 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (Calls off 2 E. L. H.) Moses—Moses! Enter Moses, reading a book, 2 E. L. H. — Come, Moses! (slapping him on the shoulder) Shut Epictetus, boy, and open the wine. (Moses turns up L.— crosses to R. H. table—gets a bottle of wine and the corkscrew.) But how came you. to entrust the saving of your sister to a stranger, boy?

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: (coming down c.) Why, Sir, I was meditating on a disputed passage, when I heard the scream; I proceeded to the spot, and by the time I had calculated the point to which the force of the current would carry Sophy, the strange gentleman, who did not seem to calculate at all, had jumped in and pulled her to the bank.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (R.) For my part, my dear, I think, what with your Epictetuses and such stuff, you'll be making a gawky of the boy. (Moses fumbling with corkscrew.) Is that the way to handle a corkscrew, sirrah?

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: The conclusion I draw—(sententiously, and poising the corkscrew.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Conclusion, quotha! Draw the cork, boy! (Moses retires to table R.) Sure the lad will never cut the figure that becomes the future head of the Primroses, warrant me, now, he'd be just as awkward at a ball or an assembly—as if he'd never had father or mother !

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Pooh, pooh! The lad's well enough—well enough!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: What a pity I did not know of this strange gentleman's visit, my dear! I might have put on my crimson Paduasoy.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Yes, and ordered thy coach, my dear!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: My coach?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: If you did not wish to have the parish children hooting after you. Dame Deborah Primrose, wife of Dr. Primrose, on a living of fifteen pounds per annum, carrying the family dinner to the hay-field, in a crimson Paduasoy!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Indeed, you used to say that it became me vastly. There was a time when you were proud to see your wife and daughters neat and handsome about you;

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Finery, my love, does not become us who have barely the means of decency,—I hardly know if it becomes even the wealthy. Consider that the nakedness of the poor might often be clothed from the trimmings of the rich.

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: (coming down R.H.) Right, Sir—I've often thought that coat-tails are a vicious superfluity.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ah! here comes our water party.

div.stage: Enter Sophia, Burchell, Olivia, Dick, and Bill, 2 E. L. H.
Dick and Bill assist Moses to place table centre of Stage, with a seat at top and on each side. (Dr. P. clasps Sophia to his heart.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: (L. E, embracing Sophia) Bless thee, my child!—bless thee! Oh, thou cruel child—to frighten thy parents to death, and spoil thy new dress!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p:
(L, Shaking Burchell warmly by the hand.) May
Heaven give you the blessing, I cannot speak. (Choked with emotion.) Now, to table, lads and lasses.

div.stage: [Seats himself at top of table L. H.—Mrs. P. at top R. H. —Bill at her side—Burchell on R. H.—Olivia L. H.— Sophia is seating herself next to Olivia.—Moses places a stool L. H. and sits by himself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, nay, girl, next to Mr. Burchell. (Sophia seats herself R. H.). Why—I declare—thy bath hath given thee quite a complexion, child.

sp.speaker: Dick
sp.p: Oh! no, it wasn't the bath; it was Mr. Burchell.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Dick! how can you?

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Ah! Didn't I see you, as I dropped behind Livy and Bill, and didn't you lean on Mr. Burchell's arm, and didn't he speak ever so softly, and didn't you get ever so red. (Runs to L., jumping on R. of Olivia.) Didn't we see her, Livy?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: I saw no such sight, saucebox.

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Ah! then it was because you were looking at the Squire in his laced coat (runs to Dr. P.) on such a fine horse, Papa! and such lots of dogs. He lifted his hat to our Livy, and she looked at him, and he looked at her (returns to Olivia), and who turned red then—eh, sister Livy?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, Dick! I never once looked at him, nor he at me; for it was just then—wasn't it, Sophia?—he caught the lash of his whip in the hawthorn tree, and was ever so long getting it out again, for I watched him.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And never once looked at him—Livy!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
Burch.
sp.stage: (Startled out of his conversation with Sophia.)
sp.p: Madam?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Deborah, Deborah, hast thou still to learn that pride must have a fall, after thy tumble from old Blackberry? They must needs ride to church last Sunday, Mr. Burchell; the girls on the wall-eyed colt, and Moses and my lady on old Blackberry—when the straps of my lady's pillion broke, and the crimson Paduasoy was landed in the mire (all laugh). Now, pass the gooseberry.

div.stage: Dick gets Olivia's guitar from tree, U. E. R. H., and gets round to L to Moses.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Dr. Primrose, Dr. Primrose, thou art incorrigible!

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.stage: on stool L. (Rising, and with much solemnity.)
sp.p:
We learn, from Athenaeus, that it was the custom among the ancients, at their banquets, to pass round a lyre, and a branch
of laurel, when each guest contributed his scholion for the entertainment—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: His scullion, child?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: His scullion, mother!—No, his scholion: so called in Greek. We have no laurel, Sir, and no lyre—hut here's sister Livy's guitar (taking it from Dick), and if you will sing a scholion. Sir (hands Burchell the guitar),—

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Well thought of, Moses: come, Mr. Burchell.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Nay, Mr. Moses, I don't know Greek, and I can't sing; so, like other inventors of tortures, you must fall the first victim to your own design.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Do, Moses: and give us something cheerful—"Death and the Lady," or '"Johnny Armstrong's Last Good Night," or "The Cruelty of Barbara Allen.

div.stage: Song by Moses,Phillip the Falconer;" by E. J. Loder — Sold by Duff and Hodgsonm, Oxford-Street.—They applaud—Moses crosses to R, and puts his stool off 2 E. R.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Most of his mother's family could sing a good song. 'Twas a common saying, in our county, that the Blenkinsops could never look straight before them; nor the Higginsons blow out a candle—that there were none of the Grograms but could sing a good song, or of the Marjorams but could tell a good tale.

div.stage: Horns without, L. H.

sp.speaker: Dick. | Bill.
sp.p: Oh! the hounds—the hounds !

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: And there bounds the poor stag!—how it sobs and strains! See, the hounds are upon its haunches—it mast turn at the brook—no, it plunges in; the dogs follow; it struggles up the opposite bank, under the pollard. Oh! here comes the hunters over the fallow—one, two, three—with the Squire leading. (Clapping her hands with delight.) Oh, brave black !—he tops the hedge like a bird—he has taken the brook in his stride. And now the stag turns—he holds the hounds at bay—look how his antlers sweep from side to side! Oh, good stag! Ah, there's a hound springing at his throat !—another, and another!—Oh! I can look no more. (Turns away, hiding her face in her hands.)

div.stage: Horn sounds a mort, L. H.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Well, for a nice, noble, genteel sport, give me stag hunting!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: The excitement of a savage, followed by the achievements of a butcher.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: But, your servant, Doctor and ladies, I have important business to attend to.
sp.stage: (Crosses to L,.—All rise and come forward.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Important business. indeed

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Truly important, I have to carry a whistle to one of Farmer Flamborough's children.

div.stage: Exit Burch. 2 R. L. H.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Important business, indeed! but as I am a living woman, here comes the Squire! Run into the house, Livy, and set me out a pair of lace pinners. No ! it's too late. Come hither, child. (Turns Olivia and Sophia about, and, arranges their dresses.) Now, hold up your heads, and remember your best curtsey.

div.stage: Enter Thornhill and Chaplain, 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Now, Frank, keep thy mouth shut, or strike me dumb if I don't unfrock you.

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Never fear me, Squire-the Vicar's one of us; and we black sheep always keep up appearances before one another.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Mrs. Primrose, I kiss your hand—ladies, I am your slave: I must welcome you to our country side, country fashion (Salutes them.) Doctor, I use a neighbour's freedom. But, egad! I forgot I had a stranger to introduce. Mrs. Primrose, let me present to you the most graceless spark of these parts — Ned Thornhill—at your service: master of an old house, a good cellar, the most musical hounds, and the thirstiest chaplain in the country. (Flicks Chaplain with his whip.) Here, Frank, make a leg and show thy breeding.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: You're welcome, Squire, and you too, Sir. The cloth is always welcome here, whatever the cut of it—(crosses to R.—aside) but I took him for the huntsman!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: This is Olivia, Squire, our eldest; and this is Sophia, our second (Squire bows); and this is our boy, Moses.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Mr. Moses, your most obedient.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: A ripe scholar, Squire, bashful as he looks.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Odso: Frank, I must turn Moses over to thee; if the ghosts of thy classics be not long ago laid in a Red Sea of claret (Retires up L.)

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Nay, I am his man. (Crosses to c.) "Arma Virumque"—hey? Mr. Moses? dost thou know thy "As in presenti? "

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Methinks I need not go far for my "Ass in presenti," in your Reverence's company.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Ha! ha! well said, Master Moses! drop him, Frank, he bites. (They reseat themselves at table—Squire L. of Olivia—Chaplain L. of Sophia—Moses R. of Sophia, facing the Squire.) I never made one of a more charming family party in my life.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p:
He considers himself one of the family, already !
Well, stranger things have happened (aside). If Squire Thornhill and this reverend gentleman, would condescend to taste our wine. (To Olivia.) Olivia, my child, wait upon Squire Thornhill. Excuse her awkwardness, she is but a poor country thing; and has not mixed in the polite world, as we have.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And can only boast her own grace, instead of the dancing-master's. (Aside)

div.stage: Olivia hands Thornhill wine.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Strike me classical; but such a Hebe is fit cupbearer for such nectar. (Drinks) Filthy stuff! (Aside.)

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Delicious! (Drinks.) Gooseberry! (Aside—with disgust.)

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Strike me stupid, Vicar, I could foreswear cards, claret, and the chase, if Miss Olivia would but condescend to turn Iphigenia to such a Cymon.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Such a what Sir, please?

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Cymon—you know.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh yes! I've read about Simple Simon in the story books.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah, you will find the girl well-read, I warrant me, Squire, I have directed her studies myself.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Especially with the mysteries of pickling, preserving, and pudding making.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: My dear, wilt thou never learn good manners?

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.stage: (Sees the Chaplain paying court to Sophia.)
sp.p: Egad, Miss Sophia—'ware honest Frank, he is the very Lovelace of parsons. Come tell us honestly Frank, suppose your mistress, the Church, on one hand, and Miss Sophia on the other—which would you be for?

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: For both, to be sure.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Right, Frank—Egad! a fine woman is worth all the priestcraft in creation,

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: How, Sir?

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: And I can prove it.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I think I should be able to prove to the contrary.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Very well Sir. (Winks to the company.)If you are for a cool argument on the subject, I accept your challenge. And first, are you for managing it analogically or dialogically?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I am for managing it rationally.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Good again, and firstly of the first—I hope you will not deny that whatever is, is—If you don't grant me that, I can go no further.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I think I can grant you that, and make the most of it.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: I hope, too, that you will grant that a part is less than the whole.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I grant that too—It is but just and reasonable.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: I hope you will not deny, that three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Nothing can be plainer.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Very well, the premises being thus settled, I proceed to observe that the concatenation of self-existence, proceeding in a reciprocal duplicate ratio, naturally produces a problematical dialogism, which in some measure proves that the essence of spirituality may be referred to the second predicable.

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: Hold, hold, I deny that. Do you think I can thus tamely submit to such heterodox doctrines?

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: What? not submit! Answer me one plain question. Do you think Aristotle right, when he says relatives are related?

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: Undoubtedly.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: If so, then answer me directly to what I propose. Whether do you judge the analytical investigation of the first part of my entheymeme deficient secundum quoad, or quoad minus? And give me your reasons, I say, directly.

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: I protest, I don't rightly comprehend the force of your reasoning; but, if it be reduced to one single proposition, I fancy it may then be answered.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Oh, Sir! your most humble servant—I find you want me to furnish you with argument and intellect too. No, Sir; there, I protest, you are too hard for me. (Moses turns up R.)

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Ha—ha—ha! Poor Moses!

div.stage: They rise and come forward, and Farm-Servant enters 2 E. R. H. and puts the table and seats backs 2 R. H.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: But, egad! in this charming company I must not forget my serious duties. I make it a point, Dr. Primrose, always to see the dogs made comfortable after their day's work. Good day to you, Doctor. Mrs. Primrose, I shall beg to wait upon you again. Young ladies, your slave. (Aside to Olivia.) You're a divinity—I love, adore you. Good bye! Master Moses, and remember, in your next argument, that the concatenation of self-existence proceeds in a reciprocal duplicate ratio, ha—ha—ha!

div.stage: Exeunt Thornhill and Chaplain bowing 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: What wit!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: What humour!

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: What good-breeding!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: He thought I'd admit his quoad minus; but I was up to him there, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, my poor boy, he used three hard words to your one. But didst thou notice, my dear, how smitten he seemed with Livy?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I'm sorry for it—sorry for it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And I hope we may soon see the day, when we shall hold up our heads with any of them. Why should the Miss Wrinklers marry great fortunes, and not our Livy and Sophy? Answer me that, Doctor?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, I see no reason, nor why Mr. Simpkins drew the £10,000 in the lottery, when we sat down with a blank.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: This is the way you always damp my girls and me, when we are in spirits. But what think you of the Squire, girls?

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: We can't think so well of him, as he thinks of himself, mama!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: And how he can talk—the more trifling the subject. the more he has to say about it. But I can't bear him, he's so impudent and familiar—and as for his swearing, its quite shocking.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: And as for argument—I don't value him not a pin. (Turns up R.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I protest he's charming—and you Doctor?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I say nothing, my dear, except this, that there's no character more contemptible than a fortune-hunting man—except a fortune-hunting woman.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Why, Dr. Primrose, what do you mean ?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nothing, my love, I give you the text, you can apply it. Livy, darling (turning towards her)—have a care!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, never fear, I'll keep watch and ward over my heart, never fear.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Thou hast more to guard than that darling—thy parents' happiness, the peace and honour of their grey hairs; bless thee, child.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Dear father.

div.stage: Enter Chaplain, 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Your servant, Doctor, and ladies. Honest Ned sent me back—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And who may honest Ned be, Sir—of whom do you speak so familiarly?

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: The Squire—'tis honest Ned, and honest Frank, with us, as you saw, Doctor, for I am highly private with him, I assure you. Honest Ned sends me back to say; that he has ordered a well-kept haunch down to the vicarage for supper, and a dozen of the yellow seal; though the gooseberry is of a delicious flavour! (Aside.) Heaven help me. And while 'tis roasting, we'll command the fiddlers for a dance on the green, at which, he prays the honour of Miss Olivia's fair hand for a minuet.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p:
There, Doctor, our Livy's hand. And who knows how it may end, Doctor? (Crosses to Chaplain) Tell Squire Thornhill Sir, that we are infinitely
beholden to his politeness, and that I and Doctor Primrose are bound—

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: No, you may leave out Doctor Primrose.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: That I and Doctor Primrose are proud of the honour he does us, and that our daughter Olivia—

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Would rather it were a roundabout, or a jig, than a minuet.

div.stage: Retires up to Sophia and Moses at back.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Hold thy peace, thou vulgar chit—will be glad to walk a minuet with him. I have taught her as well as e'er a Bath dancing-master.

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: He takes the liberty to bring with him Miss Carolina Wilhelmina Amelia Skeggs, and my Lady Blarney, two ladies of quality, now on a visit to the hall, who are very desirous to be made known to Mrs. Primrose.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: They're vastly obliging. Did I not tell you, Doctor, the family should hold up its head again?

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Ladies, your most obedient. (Bows, is going—Returns—and earnestly to Mrs. Primrose.) Look that they fold the flap over the haunch, and see that the paste be thick enough, or it plays the devil with the gravy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir; but it is not the first haunch I have seen cooked, by a great many.

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Assuredly and spare not for the currant jelly, as you love me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: As the Doctor says "jam satis."

div.stage: Exit Chap. I E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Oh! cassock, cassock—like charity, thou coverest a multitude of sins.

div.stage: Enter Burchell with the Misses Flamborough, Bill, and Dick, 2 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ha, Patty! ha, Letty! with cheeks as bright as your top-knots. Welcome, girls.

div.stage: Kisses them—They go up and shake hands with Mrs. Primrose and the girls.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: The farmer insisted on my walking down with Letty and Patty, to make his peace with you for his very excusable passion this morning.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Pooh! pooh! that's all over. Here, girls, a glass of wine. (He takes them to table R. H. and gives them wine.)

sp.speaker: Dick
sp.p: Oh! do come, and have a romp in the hay; it's such fun !

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Oh! a romp! a romp! Egad I'm with you, boys!.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh! yes a romp! Bait the bear. (Draging Moses to front.) Moses is such a capital bear.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Blind man's buff—you be blinded, Mr. Burchell.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, I know—hunt the slipper! hunt the slipper ! it's such fun.

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Yes! hunt the slipper—Come Moses!

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: Nay, I would rather read Epictetus.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Hang thee, coxcomb; to be ever poring over books is the worst of idleness.

div.stage: Olivia and Sophia take hold of their father, and place him for the game at the top of the ring.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay! but my daughters romping among the hay-cocks, like dairy-maids! Think of the family prospects, girls. (They all seat themselves, Olivia in the middle.) Ah! with their father to set such an example. What can you expect? Poor dears!—they look very happy.

div.stage: They play the game of hunt the slipper.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: There! it's with you, Patty—no, there, Papa's got it!—Mr. Burchell! Moses!—nay, one at a time. Fair play! Fair play ! Sophy !

div.stage: Enter the Squire and Miss Skeggs, the Chaplain and Lady Blarney. 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: The ladies of quality! Oh! if the earth would be so kind as to open and swallow us up!

div.stage: Turns up R.—The Squire, Miss Skeggs, Chaplain, and Lady Blarney, cross to R. H.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Capital fun, egad! I'm for hunt the slipper. (Crosses to c.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Well, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Why, I protest, child, thy blushes become thee vastly. Stand as thou art, and let me look at thee!

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Thornhill here! he must not see my face. (Retires up.)

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Mrs. Primrose, Lady Blarney and Miss Carolina Wilhelmina Amelia Skeggs.

div.stage: Miss S. and Lady B. curtsey with mock dignity.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I'm overwhelmed with confusion. But girls will be girls, your ladyships. (Aside.) It's all up with the family dignity.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I protest they're charming. Introduce us.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: This is Olivia, our eldest; if your ladyship pleases; and this is Sophia our second, under your ladyship's favour.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: There's a shape your ladyship. ( Turning Olivia round.)

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I vow and declare, they would play the devil among the sparks at Ranelagh. Lord Spindle would rave.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: And Sir Ricketts Ricketts would go distracted.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: You're a wood-nymph and your confusion brightens your charms.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Hang me! if I don't doat upon Sophia.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: And hang me ! if I would give my little Olivia here, for a bushel of Sophias.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Oh! I never,—the likeness to her Grace, the Duchess of Cinqpace—her very moral, by all that's "commy fo," your ladyship.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: The very moral of a duchess—Doctor, did you hear?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: None the more moral for that, my dear.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Strike me, ladies, a winter in town would turn Miss Sophy into a grace, and Miss Olivia into a divinity. (Retires up L.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: By jingo! you've said it, Squire. Would'st like to come up to town, child (to Olivia) and see company, and learn taste, and pictures, and Shakespeare, and the musical glasses?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, yes! my lady! I do so dote upon town, though I've never been there. I dream about it often, and all its sights and pleasures (Miss S. retires up c.) I'm tired of the hayfield and the honeysuckles, and hunt the slipper.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Livy!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: No, not of you, papa (throwing her arms round his neck.) I could not leave my papa, you know.

div.stage: Mrs. P., Miss Skeggs, and Lady Blarney come forward.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: All I know of the matter is this, that the whole rout was in amaze; his lordship turned all manner of colours; my lady fell into a swound; but Sir Tomkyn Tomkyns, drawing his sword, swore he was her's to the last drop of his blood.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Fudge!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Mr. Burchell! (Goes round to L.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Madam!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, the Duchess never told me a syllable of the matter. This you may depend on for a fact, that the next morning my Lord Duke called three times to his vally-de-sham—Jernigan! Jernigan! Jernigan!—bring me my garters.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Fudge!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Are you aware, my dear, my reader and companion has left to be married to Captain Roach, and I can assure you a proper person is no easy matter to find. To be sure, thirty pounds is a small stipend for a well-bred girl of character, that can read, write, and behave in company; as for the chits about town, there is no bearing them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Dr. Primrose—Dr. Primrose —do you hear? thirty pounds, a year, going a-begging.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: So is my wife, I can see.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Your ladyship will pardon my present presumption, but I will be bold to say that my two girls have had a pretty good education. They can read, write, and cast accounts; they understand their needle; my eldest can cut paper, and my youngest has a very pretty way of telling fortunes upon the cards.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Fudge! (Aside.)

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, we will talk with our cousin Thornhill about it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Your ladyship's vastly kind.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: And now, ladies! what do you say to a dance—a dance?

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Miss Sophia? (Offering his hand.)

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, here is a gentleman who has worked with me all day, and 'tis fit he should dance with me now.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: I can't dance—(aside to Sophia). but if ever I learn, it shall be to dance with thee. And now farewell, for I am no company for these fine ladies.

div.stage: (Exit Burchell 1 E. R. H.)

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Faugh, the clodpole!

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: And now, hey for Sir Roger de Coverley.

div.stage: Enter Flamborough and Dame, and Farm-Servant 2 E.L.H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.stage: (L.—Taking Mrs. Primrose by the hand, crosses to table R. U. E. and seat themselves.)
sp.p: Come, dame, you and I will sit on one side, and watch their harmless sport.

div.stage: [Music.
(Dance—"Roger de Coverley.")

list.item: 7. Dame ... F.-Servant.
6. Letty ... Bill.
5. Patty ... Dick.
4. Lady. B. ... Flamb.
3. Miss S. ... Moses.
2. Sophia ... Chaplain.
1. Olivia ... Thornhill.

div.stage: At the end of the Dance, half and whole turn, join hands, and circle—Curtain descends while they are dancing.

div.head: Scene I.—Music—Interior of the Vicar's Cottage.—
div.stage: Tableau: "Dressing Moses For The Fair." (After Maclise's picture.)—Fire-place 2 E. R. H.—Pair of pistols hung over the fire-place.—Door in flat, R. H.—An opening in flat, L. H., with windows backing the principal entrance, L. of opening—R. passage opening to other apartments—A table R. on which are books, writing materials, piece of beef on dish, plates,brown jug—Dr. Primrose seated on chair, R. of table, teaching Bill to read—Dick leaning on front of table, looking on—Mrs. Primrose behind table, with basin and spoon in her hand—Moses seated on chair L. C.—Sophia seated on stage B. of Moses, polishing his shoe-buckle with pocket-handkerchief—Olivia L. of Moses, arranging his hat—A towel, comb, and brush at Moses' feet L. H.—A chair 1 E. L. H. with Olivia's guitar resting against back of it—A small box with strap on Moses's lap.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Come boys!

div.stage: He takes Dick and Bill and Exits L. of opening—Mrs. Primrose Exit B. door of flat.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: There! you've made his buckles as bright as your eyes, Sophy, when Mr. Burchell opens that rusty mouth of his to let out a compliment.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Ah! who blushes reddest when a certain Squire—

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Is that the way to set a hat, Sophy? Why there's no more spirit in that pinch, than in the lop ears of Edward's—the Squire's—Spaniel—

div.stage: (Enter Mrs. Primrose R. D. Flat)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Come—come—how long wilt thou be loitering, boy?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, we must send him out a credit to the family; mama—just one more touch at his hat. There Moses! and now nobody that didn't know you, would take you for a Simpleton, (Kisses him.)

div.stage: [He rises—and Sophia puts chair against flat, and box on it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Buss me, boy. [Moses kisses her]

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: Good bye, girls—good bye, mother (going.)

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Mind don't forget my ribbons, Moses.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Never fear. (Going again.)

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p:
Bless his wits—Moses,
you're forgetting the box for the groceries—(aside), and my mantua trimmings, please, Moses.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Oh, bother! (Aside.) I'll tell mother, if you mention them again. (Going.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And the cordial waters, boy—and enquire at the potticary's for—let me see—some borax and pomecitron, and yes—two scruples of "fat musk'—remember, "fat musk," Moses—the delicatest perfume, girls—mind to ask for "fat musk," Moses.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I'll tell you what it is, if any one reminds me of anything any more, I shall go and forget everything.

div.stage: Exit opening L. in flat—The girls run to the door, looking after him.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: And a very pretty figure he cuts, dear fellow, in his thunder and lightning coat, and gosling green waistcoat.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And I hope he'll bring back a good price for the colt; we shall need it all to prepare you both for town my dears. There's the amber satin I was married in, I shall clean and cut it up to make thee a saque, Livy; and Sophy shall have a Joseph out of my crimson Paduasoy. A mother must make sacrifices for her children. (Kisses them.) And I shall see you in your coaches yet, my darlings; and then you won't be ashamed of your old mother, will you?

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Oh, no! never, mama.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: And if I am, dear mama, you have only to ask dear papa to look angry at me, if he can, and I shall be a good girl again.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah! bless you both, you're as good girls, though I say it, and as handsome as ever mother had. But thou art sadly sunburned, my Livy. These walks in Three-acre Copse, with a certain fine gentleman—

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Mamma.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: But the wash will take it all away, so get the pipkin, Sophy. (Sophia goes out R. door in flat and returns with pipkin, which she places on hob.) And you, Livy, read me the receipt, that I may see if I have forgotten anything

div.stage: Olivia takes book from table, and sits on side of table Mrs. Primrose standing on R. of her, and reads.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: "To make a wash for beautifying the skin, and removeth freckles and sunburns, and maketh the old appear young "—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, a rare wash!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p:
" With other marvellous virtues. At the wane of the moon, or when she is in the sign Virgo, take the yolks of ten eggs; of maiden-hair, rosemary, and pimpernel, each one handful; an ounce of white copperas, and four and twenty red snails." Delightful. " Let all simmer till they come to a pottle, strain, and put into a close vessel for use—It is exceeding sovereign.—Where there be no red snails to come
by, the fat of one that has been hanged, being a seventh son of a seventh son, hath as great virtue."

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, I doubt that.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: We have got snails, mamma.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: See that it simmers, Sophy.

div.stage: Sophia goes to the fire-place—Olivia places book on table.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, mama! here comes papa from the stable.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Spread yourselves, children.

div.stage: [Mrs. P. expands before fire place.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: There mamma, nobody can see a bit of the fire.

div.stage: Enter Vicar, booted, L. of opening.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Bless the man! Is he going hunting with the Squire?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I will but ride Blackberry over to the fair. (Aside.) And make a better bargain for him than Moses, methinks.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: To the fair, Charles? What hast thou to do with fairs?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I must buy two more reams of paper for my controversy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: More paper! Hast thou not spoiled paper enough already with thy deuteronomies, and bigamies, and thingamies?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Would'st thou not have been in prison already, for thy printer's bill, but that the Squire kindly lent thee the forty pounds to pay it?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: It was like him—so good and generous.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, Charles, that's not one of your books, Charles—

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: " Markham's Complete Gentlewoman," I guessed as much; doubled down at "Conceited secrets of sovereign washes for the complexion." It smells very nice— (Crosses to fire-place, Mrs. P., Sophia, and Olivia, keeping in front of him, and trying to prevent him.) —but wants stirring. [Takes up poker and knocks pipkin over.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah!

sp.speaker: Sophia | Olivia.
sp.p: Papa!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: It's my awkwardness; I always am awkward when I see one of those pipkins on the fire, and I'm afraid, my dears, I always shall be—so don't put any more there, that's good creatures.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Where we are to find four and twenty red snails again, I can't think. And how you can bear to see Livy looking like a dairy-maid, when she walks with the Squire !

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh—pray—hold thy peace—do, there's a dear good mamma.

div.stage: [Puts her hand over her mouth.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, never blush for it, child, 'tis no treason. Ah, you may stare, Doctor, but if our Squire be not as fond of our Livy, and she of him, say that Deborah Primrose has never had her own young days, that's all.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Silence! (crosses to c.) Olivia, my child (taking her hand), is this true? Has there been talk of love between thee and Squire Thornhill?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: A little, dear father.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And you have met him, and walked with him?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Sometimes.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And never told me, nor thy mother, child? It was wrong, my child, silence in such a case is deception; and she who begins by deceiving her parents, may end by dishonouring them.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, I have been very wicked, (bursts into tears.) Do not hate me, father?

div.stage: Miss Skeggs, as a Gypsey Woman, looks in at window, L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Hate thee, my child—nay, let me bless thee, rather, (lays his hand upon her head). But take care my darling, I do not like that man. He scoffs and scorns at all religion and no child of mine shall ever marry an unbeliever.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Who knows, my dear, that our Livy may not convert him?—to my knowledge, the child is well skilled in controversy.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Indeed, papa, I have read a great deal of controversy; I've read all the disputes between Thack'em and Square, in Tom Jones.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And the arguments between Robinson Crusoe and Friday the savage.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Good girl, good girl, I see you are perfectly qualified for making converts (kisses her). Now go and assist your mother to make the gooseberry pie.

div.stage: (Exit Dr. Primrose, opening L. H.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Gooseberry pie, indeed! I hope, my dears, you may come to spend your time in very different occupations from that; for I saw a ring in the candle last night, as plain as the nose on my face.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: And what do you think I dreamt of, mama?—a coffin and cross-bones; and that's the sign of a wedding all the world over.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: And there was a true lover's knot at the bottom of my teacup at breakfast.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah! let me but once see my girls fairly launched in London, and I should like to know why they should not both come to be persons of quality just as much as Miss Wilhelmina Carolina Amelia Skeggs, or my Lady Blarney? And now come, Sophy, and help me with the black puddings.

div.stage: [Exeunt Mrs. P. and Sophia, R. door flat.
Enter Miss Skeggs disguised as a Gypsey—opening L. H.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Cross the poor Gypsey's hand with a piece of silver, my pretty lady, and let her tell your fortune by the stars, or the lines of your hand.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Now go away, my good woman. Papa's very kind to the poor; but he doesn't like Gypsies. I have nothing for you.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Ah! my pretty lady; but I've something for you—it's in your fate, my pretty lady—you shall leave home shortly. (Seizing her hand.) There's the line of wealth that runs straight with the line of life—and there's one that has loved many, but loves you better than all; and there is the hunter, that holds you above his horses, and his dogs, and liberty. Ah, my pretty lady! you have a great fortune before you.

div.stage: [Still holding her hand.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Let me go, you foolish woman, or I will call mamma.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Keep your own secret, my pretty lady, and none will find it out—you have been distressed in your mind, lately; but you will soon see one who will bring you comfort, if you will only listen to love and the stars. I tell you, my pretty lady, you will leave home shortly—

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Leave home! Oh! no—no.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: And there will be a mad gallop, and a happy wedding, and a happy bringing home of the bride; but you must not cross the stars, for love is true, and the crooked is straight, and a bold course is a good course, my pretty lady —so cross the poor Gypsey's hand with a piece of silver, and she will tell you more that she learns from the stars.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: No, no—there (gives money). Now, go, my good woman—(forcing a laugh)—I have heard quite enough nonsense for to-day.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Don't mock the stars, my pretty lady,—I see a gay coach—and a bold, merry gentleman—and a yielding, dark lady,—so don't cross the stars, for they bode you great fortunes.

div.stage: Exit L opening in flat.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p:
What a little fool I am to listen to such jargon! She shoots her words at random; and for half the girls in the village, they would hit the mark as well as me.—A bold
gentleman—a mad gallop!—why, any one would think I was going to run away and get married!

div.stage: Enter Groom L opening.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: A letter for Mrs. Primrose. (Olivia takes it.) And are you Miss Primrose, Ma'am?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: Then here's a letter for you too, Miss. (Gives it, and Exit L.)

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Edward's hand (going to open it-) But I am doing wrong to open it; and yet, what harm can there be in just looking at it? I can't answer it unless I read it; and perhaps it is to tell me that he loves me, and that he intends to ask my father's consent to the avowal of it—I will open it—but I fear I am wrong. (Pauses, and then tears it open. Reads.) "Meet me this evening, by the Three-acre Copse —the old spot. To-night we must part, or be blessed for ever. I shall expect you at nine."—At nightfall?—and alone? That Gypsey's words come back—"You will leave home shortly." Pshaw!—what a coward I am!—and to distrust Edward thus ! Yes, I will be there, and shew him how wicked we have both been. He shall come with me to my father. We will have no more of these secret meetings. Either we will love honestly, and before the world, or we will love no longer. (Calls at door R.) Mamma—mamma!

div.stage: (Enter Mrs. Primrose R door flat.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Well, child?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: A letter from the Hall, mamma.

div.stage: [Gives the letter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: No doubt to arrange for your visit to town, my child. I trust their ladyships will leave me time to make up the amber satin and the crimson Paduasoy. (Opens the letter and reads.) "Dearest Madam " — How respectful and affectionate at the same time "—I regret much that the receipt of the enclosed letter has so alarmed my friends, Miss Skeggs and Lady Blarney, that they have not only abandoned their intention of taking your amiable daughters under their protection"—Oh, gracious!—"but have themselves quitted my house this morning suddenly and apparently in anger. I am only anxious that the writer of the enclosed should be discovered, and punished as he deserves. " Your devoted servant, " Edward Thornhill." — Alack, alack!—the prospects of the family ruined and undone, and I shan't see you ladies of quality after all—and there's fifty pounds, ten shillings, a year, as good as lost to the family for ever!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: But the enclosed letter, mamma?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, read it child,

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: " To the ladies of quality at Squire Thornhill's.—The writer of this is a friend of innocence"—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Innocence, quotha!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: " He is informed that you have some intention of bringing to town two young ladies of his acquaintance"—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: His acquaintance! Marry, come up, my dirty cousin.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: " In the character of companions. As he would not have simplicity imposed on, or virtue contaminated, he must offer his opinion that such a step would have dangerous consequences. So take the admonitions of a friend, against introducing infamy and vice into retreats where peace and innocence have hitherto resided."

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Here's a Gunpowder Plot! Oh! I shall faint!—vice and infamy?—my daughters! Oh! support me, my child.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Yes, I was sure I knew the hand—why it is—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Whose? Let me but find out.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Mr. Burchell's, as I live, mamma!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And so it is!—(looking at the letter.) There are his sneaking "g's" with the short tails, and his meanspirited "i's" with no dots to 'em. The profligate!—oh, the double-distilled sinner!—Sophy, Sophy! come and see what a viper it was that pulled you out of the water.

div.stage: Exit, followed by Olivia.—(Opening in flat R.H.

div.head: Scene II.—
div.stage: The Market-place, with a fair going on—Lads and lasses in holiday dresses, farmers, &c.—A drinking-booth, R. H. U. E. with a table and forms outside—Ephraim Jenkinson, is discovered on a raised platform, with a speaking trumpet, selling drugs as a quack doctor, in a robe and long beard, in centre of the stage, his Jack Pudding standing on his left, with box of medicines, bottles, pills, &c. E. —The Scene opens to music-gongs beating, shouts, laugh' ing, &c.—Jack Pudding blows the horn,

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p:
Hey, hey hey!—holloa! here I am—Don Waltero Von Clatterbank, High German Doctor, native of Arabia Deserts, seventh son of a seventh son; who has studied under Galen, Hippocrates, Paracelsus, and Albumezar. All persons, young or old, blind or lame, deaf or dumb, curable or incurable—come here for cure of all cephalalgias, paralytic paroxysms, palpitations of the pericardium, syncopes, vertiginous vapours, hydrocephalous dysentries, odontalgic or podagrical inflammations, the hogpox, the hen-pox, the chicken-pox, or the small pox; ascites, ascarides, anasarca, or anthropophagi.—(Jack Pudding blows
the horn—the crowd laugh—Farmer and Dame Flamborough, and their daughters, come down R. H.—Jenkinson, pointing to Dame F.)—Now, there's an old lady suffering from an oesophagus in her outacousticon.

sp.speaker: Dame F.
sp.p: Lord preserve us! I do feel queerish.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Let her buy a box of my anti-pamphustic pills, the same that cured Prester-John's Jugler's wife of a dogmatism in her elbow, of which she died. (Jack Pudding blows horn) The box is only sixpence; see the effect. Here John, take a pill.

div.stage: (Jack Pudding takes pills.)

sp.speaker: Dame F.
sp.p: Here, doctor, my good man is woundily troubled with the falling sickness after market days.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: And here is my balsamum swallosordusticum, good against all cuts and green wounds. If any honest man among you has hurt himself with sword, gun, or pitchfork, spit, jack, or gridiron, glass-bottle, or pint-pot, one application of the balsam will cure him, without sending to an illiterate surgeon.

div.stage: Jack Pudding blows the horn. Shouts, &c.—Enter Moses, 1 E. L. H.)

sp.speaker: Farmer F.
sp.p: Ah! them doctors does take a plaguy long time, and wonderful sight o' money. Here's for thy balsam, doctor.

div.stage: [Several buy.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: This is the "Unguentum cataphon," which is sovereign for all strains, sprains, and bruises. It was this that prevented the old woman at Exeter from running into a wine cellar, and cured the Morocco ambassador of a lapsus linguæ.

div.stage: [Jack Pudding blows horn, and several buy)

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Lapsus lingua? I must protest—

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: And here's the secret of secrets, the "Tankapon Tolos," that performed the wonderful cure on Captain Nonsuch, of the Non-nomen galley, in the service of the Emperor of Terra Incognita, who had a cannon ball lodged in his little finger; likewise the carpenter of the same ship, who had accidently swallowed a handspike.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: No ! that I can't swallow.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Here's a simpleton doesn't believe. If I hadn't so many patients waiting inside, I could show him the very identical—

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Carpenter?

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: No—handspike!

div.stage: [Exit through curtain into his booth, 2 E. L. H., followed by Jack Pudding.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p:
That man must be an impostor! How can a cannon ball lodge in a little finger? The less cannot contain the greater. What a busy scene (looking about him). "Plethousē agorā" as Xenophon says. I shant have much difficulty in finding a customer for the colt, I dare say. The
sharpers shall find they've no ignoramus to deal with, but a young man who has studied the humanities.

div.stage: (Enter Jenkinson from his booth, having taken off his beard and gown, aud looking like a young man.)

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: A wonderful man! A wonderful man!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Ah, a patient of that impudent quack doctor.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Quack doctor, Sir? Would there were more such! One draught of his aqua soliginus has cured me of a sweating sickness, that was on me now these six years; and carried a large imposthume off my throat, that scarce let me eat, drink, or sleep, except in an upright posture—and now it is gone as clean—saving your presence—as (picks his pocket) that, Sir! Oh, a wonderful man! I came here at full length in a cart, but I shall ride back as upright as a gate-post, if I can but come by a horse.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: A customer for the colt,—he seems a simple fellow. I have a horse to sell, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Oh! but I warrant me you are one of those cozening horse jockies that take-in poor honest folk. I know no more of horses than you do of Greek.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Nay—(aside) but I must appear simple—I assure you, Sir, that you need not fear being cozened by me. I have a good stout colt for sale, that has been worked in the plough these two years—you can but step aside and look at him.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Well, as for that, I don't care if I do; but, Lord bless me! I was forgetting my wares.

div.stage: (Goes to his booth, 2 E. L. H., and brings box.)

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: What have you there?

sp.speaker: Jen.
Moses.
sp.p: Nay, my good man, I am as honest as thyself— though, perhaps, not quite such a simpleton (aside).

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Well, I don't care if I do look at thy horse—(aside) and you may say good bye to him, my ben cull. But you're sure he's quiet to ride and drive?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I've driven him myself, and I am not one that driveth furiously; and you may believe he's quiet to ride, when I tell you he's carried my mother, an old lady, and never thrown her. (Aside.) It's true, she tumbled off once —but that was her fault, and not the colt's.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Then, I don't care if I say a bargain. How much is it to be. I don't like paying more than ten guineas.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: (Aside) He's not worth half the money.—You shall name your own price—(aside) and then nobody can say I cheated him.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: What say you to nine guineas—and the odd halfguinea for saddle and bridle?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Nay, I would not drive a hard bargain—I'm content.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Stop a bit, and I'll give the money. (Sits on his box, and pretends to search his pockets.) Eh?—oh, Lord!—nay, 'tis t'other pocket—No—oh, Lord! I'm a ruined man—I be robbed—thieves!—I be robbed—

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Robbed? This comes of carrying money; "Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator," as Juvenal says. But I will lend thee enough to take thee home again.

div.stage: [Going to put his hand into his pocket.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (Prevents him.) Nay, good young man — I have friends enow in this place who will do that for me. It is the loss of the horse that vexes me. Hold!—perhaps, though I can no longer buy, you may be willing to make a barter?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Why, the practice of barter was much used amongst the ancients; and, indeed, the Lacedemonians had no coined money until after the time of Lycurgus, as you are aware.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Nan—I can't say I know the family. But will you exchange your horse against my wares? There's a good twelve pounds worth of 'em.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: What are they? Deprome—that is, bring them forth.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (Opens his box.) A gross of green spectacles—fine pebbles, and silver rims.

div.stage: [Taking a pair out of case,

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: A gross of green spectacles.

div.stage: [Taking a pair.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: A dozen-dozen.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Let's see (aside, calculates)—twelve times twelve is—and twenty-one's into—go—yes, a capital bargain! I accept —you take the colt, and I'll take the spectacles.

div.stage: (Offering to take the box.)

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Nay, nay—I'll give you the box when you've given me the colt—so, come!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: A gross of green spectacles! Huzza! (Aside.) I'll retail them for twice the money. "Nocte pluit totâ redeunt spectacula mane "—" There come back spectacles a many." Ha, ha! the silly fellow! Well, it's not my fau't —he will cheat himself—ha, ha! Oh, Moses is a simpleton, is he? Moses can't make a bargain, can't he?

div.stage: (Exit 1 E. R. H.)

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Of all the green spectacles ever sold, I must say you're the greenest.

div.stage: Enter Miss Skeggs, dressed as a Gypsey, 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Hist, Capting! Bing back when you're nabbed the prancer.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Ah, Molly!—more devil's business afoot, that thou art here on the Roumany lay?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Bing back, and we'll go shares. (Exit Jen. with box, I E. R. H.) —(To the rustics.) Cross the poor Gypsey's hand with a piece of silver, my pretty maids, and I'll tell your fortunes.

div.stage: [Retires to back with Patty and Letty Flamborough.)
Enter Squire Thornhill and Chaplain, 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: (R.) Not a decent nag or a pretty wench in the fair!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: (L.) Hang thy horse face and sheep's eyes! Canst see the Gypsey wench I told thee to mark for me?

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: (Looking and pointing to Miss Skeggs.) Yonder she is—and a likely lass too.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Then drop thy sodden carcass into that booth (pointing R.) till I call thee—I have business here.

sp.speaker: Chap.
sp.p: Aha! You run roguish, Squire! (Squire lifts his whip angrily—he bows humbly.) Nay, I trust I know my place. I will solace myself with a pipe and a pint of home-brewed, and meditate over next Sunday's sermon.

div.stage: (Exit into booth, U. E. R.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: (comes forward R.) Ha! honest Ned, 'tis all right! I've seen your charmer—dropped the word—and now her head's buzzing with the notion of a leap into a post-chaise and matrimony. The sixth of us, Squire. Ha, ha!—(bitterly) one down and t'other come on! (sighs and stops.) Six of us poor girls!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: That will do—and now off with you by the first stage to London, and see all ready in the old place. (Miss Skeggs stands irresolutely.) What's the woman staring at? D'ye hear me?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Yes, yes! But, I say, Ned, must she go?—come now!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Must she? Speak out—what are you stammering at?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Oh, Ned! she's not what we were. I was about the cottage all this morning—and her pretty ways, and that white-headed old man,—and I saw her at his knee—and he blessed her. I've had that old man's face before my eyes, and his prayer in my ears, ever since—and it frightens me, Ned!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Pooh! Molly, this is something new—you're not half old or ugly enough for psalm-singing yet. Drink a glass of brandy, and drown your new-born babe of a conscience, old girl!

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p:
I've tried that, but it will whisper me, Ned. I
had a father myself—an old man—but he never blessed me —and I suppose he never will now (mournfully).

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Sink the whimpering slut! Have you given my message to Jenkinson?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Oh, Ned, Ned! drop this pursuit—it is not too late—I have not given any orders for the chaise and men yet.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Curse you ! is this the way you serve me? I must do my own dirty work, must I, and be hanged to you?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Oh, Ned! you once said you loved me!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Stand aside, you snivelling jade, I say!

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Oh, Ned—Ned! (tries to take his hand.)

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: (thrusts her aside, and crosses to R.) Stand aside, or I'll lash you like a hound!

div.stage: (Exit 1 E. R. H.)

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: I will do my best to save the poor thing yet. That moody Burchell is about the fair,—I won't betray Ned —but he doesn't take his own carriage and servant for this job; and if the Captain can be laid by the heels, all may be safe yet. Yes, yes—I've done the mischief—I'll repair it. (Running into booth, U. E. R. H.) A glass of brandy there!

div.stage: (Re-enter Miss Skeggs, following Burchell, 2 E. R. H.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: I tell thee, wench, I am in no humour to listen to thy fooleries.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: And I tell you, that those who are too proud to listen may be too late to learn. You know Dr. Primrose— one of his daughters is in danger.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Ha! Sophia?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: No—the other. See that she does not leave the house at dusk to-night. Be about the lane that skirts the Three-acre Copse—and armed. You carry a sword?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: My stick will do as good service—but who—

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Ask no questions, for I cannot answer them. You see yon ill-looking fellow with the silly lad, the Vicar's son?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: My friend Moses—well?

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Do not lose sight of that man. If you see him about the spot I spoke of, seize him—knock him down if he resist—he is there for no good purpose.

div.stage: (Crosses to L.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: But I must know more of this.

sp.speaker: Miss S.
sp.p: Not a word. If you are a wise man, you will not need it. If you are a bold man, you will want all your courage. It's no use to follow me. If I say "Mum," neither whips, stocks, nor darbies can get a word out of me. Be alive, and good luck to you.

div.stage: (Exit 1 E. L. H.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p:
This is strange! There is some wickedness on foot, or why my cool reception from Mrs. Primrose and Sophia? Thornhill is at the bottom of this. I'll be on the watch, as this Gypsey tells me. (Looking R.) So, that is the
man I've to have an eye on—as hanging a look as ever graced the Old Bailey dock. Ware hawk! Egad! I like this adventure—it stirs my phlegmatic blood. I have not felt so like old times since I leapt into the brook after my Sophia—(feels his pulse)—on the gallop, by all that's lively —(poising his stick)—and woe to the wight that comes within sweep of my old friend here!

div.stage: Exit 1 E. R. H.
Enter Dr. Primrose 1 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! Moses seems to have got a customer. Poor lad! he little thinks his old father is in the fair, selling too. I've had no offer for old Blackberry—he's not an attractive horse—his wall-eye gives an absurd expression to his countenance. I ought to get four guineas for him, I believe; but I'm no great judge. I hope the money will be turned to a good account. I shall not be sorry to get the girls away to London. Livy's fancy for that jackanapes of a Squire grieves me. He's a bad man—I feel he is—and she loves him—she loves him ! ((Seats himself on form R. of table.)

div.stage: Enter Jenkinson, followed by Burchell cautiously, 1 E. R. H.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: I've disposed of the nag to one of my pals—so now to put on a fresh face to catch a fresh cully.

div.stage: Exit 2 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: That's my scoundrel! I'll sit down here till he cames out. (Seats himself L. of table, and recognises the Dr.) Ha, Doctor! in a fair, of all strange places!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Yes, here I am, Mr. Burchell, "to catch the manners living as they rise," as the ingenious Mr. Pope hath it. I often think we divines mix too little with the crowd. How are we to learn the secrets of the enemy's camp, unless we come out, now and then, to reconnoitre it?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (aside.) Shall I tell him? And are you here solely for philosophic observation, Doctor?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, not altogether. I've my secret, Mr. Burchell; but I think I may trust you. You know the girls start for London?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (aside.) He knows nothing of my letter, then.— Yes, Sir, I grieved to hear of it.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: They must rub off their rust, poor things. My wife's a good, notable woman, but she's a thought rusty herself. However, to travel costs money—and so I'm here to raise the wind a little, Mr. Burchell.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: How, Sir?

div.stage: Re-enter Jenkinson from his booth, dressed as an old man, with a large book, 2 E. L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p:
The fact is, we are selling our stud. I didn't put
much trust in poor Moses, who has it in charge to dispose of the colt; so, without his knowing it, I've come to tell old Blackberry myself. With your leave, I'll call for a pipe.

sp.speaker: Burch.
