sp.p: I will join you in one, Sir, with all my heart. Here, landlord, pipes, and a pint of your mildest ale.

div.stage: Enter Landlord, with pipes, jug of ale, two horns, and candle, from booth R.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (who has been listening.) The old Doctor come out horse-dealing! Bless his venerable viridity!—Just the sort of customer I like. If the son was green, I should think the father was two shades greener at least. Your great scholars always are the easiest to cozen. I've one bit of book learning—(crosses, and seats himself R. of Dr.)—'tis a famous bait—so now for it. (Opens his book, and pretends to read with great attention.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (perceiving him.') A venerable man that, Mr. Burchell.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Very. (Aside.) My knave does not make his appearance.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: How absorbed he is! A scholar that, Mr. Burchell, as sure as my name's Dr. Primrose.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: (abstracted.) I dare say. (Aside.) He has certainly not come out. If I could but peep into the booth— the canvass is open. Excuse me one moment, Dr. Primrose. (Rises, and goes into booth 2 E. L. H . )

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Primrose? Did I hear aright? May I ask, with much respect, any relation of the famous Dr. Primrose, that courageous champion of the Church?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (Rises L. C.) Sir, your applause adds to the pleasure your appearance has already excited. You behold that Dr. Primrose—that courageous champion, as you are pleased to call me—though I would rather say, that unfortunate divine, who has so long fought in vain, though perhaps not without learning, against the deuterognomy of the age.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (Rises R. C.) I fear I have been too familiar; but you will forgive my curiosity—I beg pardon—

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: No offence, my dear Sir—no offence. I trust you will accept my friendship, Sir, as you have my esteem already. (Aside.) Charming person!

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: And do I indeed behold? that glorious pillar of unshaken orthodoxy?—do I indeed behold?— "

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: You overpower me. Ah! Sir, the world does not share your opinions.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p:
The world, Sir? The world is in its dotage. (Aside.) And now for my bit of book learning. The cosmogony or creation of the world has puzzled philosophers in all ages Sanconiathon Manethon, Berosus, and Ocellus Lucanus,
have all attempted it in vain. Manethon, also, who lived about the time of Nebuchadon-asser—" asser" being a Syriac word usually applied as a surname to the kings of that country, as Nabon-asser, Teglad-Phæl-asser—formed a conjecture equally absurd. But I ask pardon, Sir—I am straying from the question.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: (aside.') So he is a little; but he's a most ripe scholar. Sir, I honour your learning; and if I had not business to attend to, I would sit and discuss the cosmogony all day.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: What, Sir! have philosophers like you business at a fair? But it is odd enough, so have I.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: You'll laugh when you learn I've come here to sell a horse.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: And you'll smile when you hear that I have come to buy one.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: If I could sell old Blackberry to carry such a learned rider!

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: You shall, Sir—what is your price?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I believe he is worth four guineas.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Say six, worthy Sir—I must give six.

div.stage: Enter Landlord from booth R.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, if you will—but I should have been content with four.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (producing pocket-book, and taking out note.) Six—six —here, landlord, can you give me gold for this fifty pound note?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.p: Nay, not I—I've ne'er so much gold in the world, nor will you easily get it.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: This is awkward; but hold—your cure is hard by. Do you know one Farmer Flamborough of your part of this country?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: My next-door neighbour.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Capital! Then you shall have a draft upon him, payable at sight. (Calls into booth.) Pen and ink, landlord. And let me tell you, he is as warm a man as any within five miles round.

div.stage: Enter Landlord with pen and ink.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (sits at table and writes.) Honest Solomon and I have been acquainted many years. I remember I always beat him at three jumps; but he could hop upon one leg farther than I. (Comes down R.) Here is a draft.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And yonder stands old Blackberry, little dreaming of the learned load he is henceforth to trot under.

div.stage: [Takes draft.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Ah, Sir! the horse that has carried a pillar of the Church (crosses to L.) must be up to any weight. Heaven bless you, most reverend Sir! I trust we may meet again.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And finish our argument on the cosmogony, for I don't agree with Manethon myself.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: (aside.) And now for the Squire's job. Lord! to think how far a little learning may go when turned to good account.

div.stage: Exit Jen. 1 E . L . H .
Dr. P. beckons Landlord, and pays him at table R.
Re-enter Burchell from booth.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: The rogue has given me the slip. The booth is empty—and yet I watched like a ferret at a rabbit-hole. I must make a cast for the scent. Good bye, Doctor, for the present!

div.stage: Exit 1 E. R. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Now for home again. I've made a famous bargain. How astonished poor Moses will be—poor lad ! I dare say he has been vilely cozened—poor lad!—vilely cozened—poor lad!

div.stage: (Enter Moses (1 E. R. H.) with box of spectacles.)

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! I'm afraid I've been a sad rogue to take that poor simpleton's valuable wares. But barter is barter; and I dare say the Lacedemonians always took as much as they could get. Father thought I should be cheated. How I shall crow over him, and all of them. Cheated indeed! I think after such a bargain I may indulge a little, as I have a long walk before me. Here, landlord, half a pint of your smallest ale—or say a pint—yes. a pint —and quick, do you hear.

div.stage: Exit into booth R. H.
The Scene Closes.

div.head: Scene III.—A Woodland Road by the Three-acre Copse.
div.stage: [Lights half-down.]
Enter Thornhill (R.) and Jenkinson (L.) meeting.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Is all ready? Your men posted to keep off intruders? (Jenkinson nods.)—The chaise-and-four at the Cross Roads? (Jenkinson nods.)—You did not tell the people at the Wheatsheaf for whom you were hiring it? (Jenkinson shakes his head.)—You have procured me a false license, and a rogue to play priest? (Jenkinson nods.)—You'll find the sorrel mare in the Copse; she'll carry you across country to the Moat house in two hours' hard riding. Don't press her over the fallows, mind, for she's worth two hundred. (Jenkinson nods.) And, now, off to your hiding-place—if any one interrupts us, use your pistols; I'll bear you harmless. (Jenkinson shrugs his shoulders)—Has Jack Ketch slit thy tongue as well as thine ears, man, that thou art all nods, and winks, and shrugs, instead of words?

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p:
(L.) I daren't trust my tongue, Squire, lest it should let out what I think of this business. If it were taking a purse
now, or cracking a crib—but carrying off a poor young innocent lamb—

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Pshaw! are all my knaves turned canters? Curse me if I shan't be throwing up the whites of my own eyes next. To thy post rogue—and remember, if thou attempt to play me false, I have that will hang thee ten times over.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: That's true. You have the advantage of me. I have offended the Law—you, Squire, have only offended the Law-giver.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: So, every rogue has his fling in my teeth. But who's afraid?—this is my grand coup of all. The rest were half-ruined to my hand. 'Twas but first come, first served, with them. But Olivia— young, lovely, and good—egad, 'tis that gives the smack to this adventure. Innocence—pshaw! What is it? The mask that hypocrisy puts on cowardice! She must be married, must she? She shall be married—ha, ha!—noosed with a rotten halter. And yet there are moments when I feel as I never felt yet. The thought of that old man will cross me; and sink me if I don't sometimes fancy I love the girl as well as desire her. She is here! My Olivia!

div.stage: Enter Olivia (L.)—she rushes to Thornhill, and flings her-self in his arms.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: (L.) Oh, Edward, Edward! I am a lost, wicked, wretched girl.

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: (R.) What! my own darling wretched? Who has dared—

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, hush, hush, Edward—'tis my own fault—I should not he here. They do not know at home what I am doing: my father blessed me to-day; and when his dear hand was upon my head, and his kind eyes looked into mine —and his good old voice trembled as he called me his darling—I knew how wicked I had been, and determined to see you no more, till he knew and sanctioned our love. You will ask me of him, Edward ?

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: It is useless—he misjudges me too much. Time alone can overcome his prejudice.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Then let us wait till he learns, as I have learnt, how good and kind you are, and that your rough ways and wild words are but bad habits that I can soon cure you of. You know you will not be so loud, and hard, and proud any longer, when you have your little Livy to love and care for, and chide you, Edward—for mind, I shall be a very strict schoolmistress.

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: And so you shall, my darling, and rate me when I bolt over the ropes, as I rate one of my hounds for false chiding.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Then you will wait till my father knows you better?

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: Nay, what hope is there in that, when you know he designs you for another, that Farmer Williams?—a fit husband for one who has graces to adorn a coronet!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: It would break my heart to marry any but you. You know it would—so why not wait in patience?

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: Wait! my passion for you, Olivia, cannot wait; you have made a new man of me already, by your love. Think what I shall be as your husband. Come, dearest, cannot you trust yourself with me?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Trust myself? oh yes! But where, Edward? whither would you take me?

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: Away from hence, but for a few days (she recoils from him)—a few hours, perhaps; only for the time required to make you my wife. All is prepared for our union, Olivia, at my seat, only a few miles from hence.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: No Edward, it is not thus a woman should pass from a father's arms to those of a husband. How can a blessing rest on the double life, that begins in flight and deception. I love you, I do indeed, but I love them too (pointing L.), and I cannot bear to think of them to-night. They are all at home now, supper is ready, my father is by the fire-side, and would be smiling, were his little Livy there to cheer him. But she comes not—my mother rises and goes to the door, and looks out upon the night, but Livy does not come; so the hours pass on, and expectation has grown into wonder, and still Livy does not come—Oh yes, she does, father, I will go back.

div.stage: (Turns to go—the Squire seizes her.)

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: Hear me, my Olivia, I have not come here to hear pretty stories, or to see how charming you look with those pearls in your eyes, and that colour in your cheeks—I am come for my love—for my wife, if you will—and I am prepared to use force, if force is necessary; so make up your mind to submit to what you cannot prevent, so come, I say!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, help ! Edward, Edward, I dare not! Father, father!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: My wife, my wife!

div.stage: [Kisses her passionately, as he forces her off R. H.
Enter Jenkinson (L.)

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Just in time, or that stout fellow, yonder, with the cudgel, would have been in on him. Ha, he has bowled down my two aid-de-camps like nine-pins. He comes this way—so!

div.stage: Enter Burchell (L.)

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Not a step, or you're a dead man.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Stand aside, scoundrel!

div.stage: [Jenkinson fires; at the same time Burchell strikes up the pistol with his stick, knocks Jenkinson down, jumps over him, and looks R.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Too late—too late. They drive off. Fire and fury!—had I not wasted time in searching the fair for this scoundrel, I should have saved her. Is he dead, I wonder? (Examines Jen., and takes pistol from his belt.) I hope I have not cheated the gallows.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Eh?—where?—what? I must say, Sir, you're as good a back-hand as Figg himself.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Rascal!—whither is that chaise bound?

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Excuse me, Sir—honour to my friend. (Rises.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Honour among thieves, truly, A bargain with thee. Tell me who it was carried off that young lady —whither they have gone—and what is his design. If thou make a clean breast of it, I spare thee, and use thee. If not, thou swing'st.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Needs must when the hangman drives. The gentleman—heaven save the mark!—was Ned Thornhill; as great a rogue, saving your presence, as any here. The lady you know. They are bound for the Moat-house, a score of miles from here—and their design is to ruin her, under pretext of marriage.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: The double-dyed villain!

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: There is the mock license, and at the Moat-house waits the mock priest. She loves him, and will tumble into the snare as innocently as the cushat into a gin.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Twenty miles! I shall be too late to undo this work of villany.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: And no ways welcome, perhaps: besides, the house is guarded—you cannot gain admission.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: True—true!

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: There's the Squire's sorrel mare, in the Copse, can beat them to the Moat-house. But what then?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Harkye! You carry word to the Vicar that his daughter is gone—say Burchell sent thee. I will take the sorrel, and do my best to prevent mischief. But give me the forged license.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: And here is the pass for the mock priest.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Does Thornhill know him ?

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: No; he is a new hand, a friend of mine—college-bred, but has had his troubles.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Then the false parson's gown may cover a true priest for once—'tis generally the other way,—and now, away with you!

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Well! I feel a kind of a relish in helping an honest action!

div.stage: (Exit L.)

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Let me see!—the Bishop is at Lord Carberry's only five miles off. I may save her—and if she loves this graceless dog, perhaps save him too; I'll try it; if I break Sorrel's wind, 'twill be in a better cause than fox-hunting!

div.stage: (Exit R.)

div.head: Scene IV.—
div.stage: Interior of Vicar's Cottage, with table R. and candles.—Arm-chair L. of table.—Small table L with guitar on it —Pistols hanging up over fire-place. Mrs. Primrose and Sophia, with Dick and Bill.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: How late your father is to-night, children! I hope his wits have not gone wandering after his deuteronomies, forsooth! and that he be not now sitting on the side of a ditch, with old Blackberry kicking up his heels over Plashy Common.

sp.speaker: Sophy
sp.p: Hark! I hear papa's footstep.

div.stage: (Enter Vicar L. D. F.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ha, Dame!—ha, Sophy!—ha, boys!

sp.speaker: Dick
sp.p: What have you brought me for a fairing, papa?

sp.speaker: Bill.
sp.p: And me, papa?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Why, Bill, as thou art an industrious lad at thy books, I have brought thee a large bit of gingerbread without any letters. And as thou, Dick, art an idle rogue, I have brought thee thy letters without any gingerbread. But where's my Livy?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: The girl is romantic, and loves walks in the twilight—I did so myself at her age.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: She will be here soon, bless her! Ah, Deborah! what would our cottage be without her bright face and merry laughter? I love you all—but Livy is the apple of my old eyes!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: I trust nothing has happened to Moses. I warrant he will bring back a good price for the colt—and good need, for I shall have a world of fine things to buy for the girls' journey to London.

sp.speaker: Sophy
sp.p: Nay, mama, you forget.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah, bless my stupid brains! so I did. Alas! my dear, all our hopes are ruined;—our girls are not to have their Town polishing after all—the more's the pity!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Thank our stars for it!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Some evil-disposed person has aspersed them to their Ladyships—aspersed the daughters of Deborah Primrose—marry come up!—as though we had not our reputations like richer folks, though we have come down from keeping our carriage!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Aspersions, say'st thou, Dame? Who has been wicked enough ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Who but that dangling, snarling, good-for-nothing Burchell!

sp.speaker: Sophy.
sp.p: Mama!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Burchell? I would have given bail for his honesty! —but "fronti nulla fides!"

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: We have it under his own hand, Dr. Primrose— an insinuating, indirect, round-about-the-bush letter, Dr. Primrose.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I grieve to hear it, my dear—as I always do at everything that makes me think worse of my fellow-creatures. But never mind—we are well rid of him. Cheer up, Sophy darling!

sp.speaker: Sophy.
sp.p: Oh! I am sure I never cared for him, papa—never! —I hated him!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Poor child! poor child !—but a truce to gloomy thoughts! Dick, run out and look for Livy—you'll be sure to find her on the Common, among the purple heather and golden broom.

sp.speaker: Dick
sp.p: And I'll put Blackberry into the stable-mayn't I, papa, as Moses isn't here?

div.stage: Exit Dick L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ha, ha! Blackberry into the stable!—that may scarce be—ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Why, my dear?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: For a very good reason, my love—there's no Blackberry to put into the stable.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: No Blackberry!—why, thou hast not gone and lost thy horse, Charles?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Lost him! Ha, ha! No, wife—but sold him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Sold him! Sold Blackberry? What hast thou got for him?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Six guineas, wife, and he was worth but four, on the authority of Farmer Flamborough (taking draft from pocket). Here 'tis, a draft on neighbour Flamborough. Here, Bill, run and get the money, 'tis but a step.

div.stage: Exit Bill L. D. F. with draft.

sp.speaker: Sophy.
sp.p: Here comes Moses, papa.

div.stage: Enter Moses, carrying deal box, L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Welcome, Moses, welcome! Well, my boy, what have you brought us from the fair?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: First and foremost, I have brought you myself.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But the colt, boy, the colt.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: I've sold him, father, and pretty well, I flatter myself. I've sold him, saddle, bridle, and all, for ten guineas.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: A great price, I protest—ten guineas!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Well done, indeed—the money, boy, the money.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Why, Sir, I've brought back no money.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah! a draft, doubtless, like your father.

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: No; but I've got a great bargain.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Good lad! but what is this bargain? Let's see!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: A gross of green spectacles, with silver rims and shagreen cases. (Opening box triumphantly.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: A gross of green spectacles! and you have parted with the colt, and brought us nothing but a gross of paltry green spectacles.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Dear mother, why won't you listen to reason, I got them a dead bargain, I can tell you. The silver rims alone would sell for twice the money.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Silver rims, indeed! they won't sell for half the money as old silver, at five shillings the ounce.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Make yourself quite easy about the rims, my dear, they're only copper varnished over, and not worth sixpence.

div.stage: [Moses turns up R. and places box at back—Puts his hand in his pocket and misses his handkerchief.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Not silver?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: No more silver than your saucepan.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: The blockhead has been cozened, he should have known his company better.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Excuse me, my dear, he should not have known them at all.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Give me the trash, I'll throw it into the fire.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: There again, you are wrong, my dear, for though they are copper we will keep them by us, for copper spectacles, you know, are better than nothing. Ah, Moses, Moses, youth-like, thou hast trusted to appearances! I expected this, 'tis lucky I sold Blackberry myself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Thy father did not let himself be thus cozened, I warrant me.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, Deborah, he has not my experience, thou knowest, we must allow for his years. I dealt with a scholar and a philosopher, though I did not clearly apprehend his doctrine of Cosmogony.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And what had his mahogany to do with the selling of a horse?

div.stage: Enter Bill, with Flamborough. (L. D. F.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Ah! Here comes the Farmer to pay the draft.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Ecod! Vicar—I'm main sorry, but you may e'en use the draft to light your pipe, for all its good for.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Not good ?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Eh?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p:
A vorgery of that rogue, Ephraim Jenkinson's, the greatest rascal unhung. He's zold me a horse, and he's stole me a horse; and now he's vorged my name! Never was such a play-actor in rogue's parts. He's highwayman,
vorger, coiner, burglar, juggler, and quack doctor, just as he likes.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: A quack doctor!—a young man?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay—an old venerable man.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Ecod! he's as many ages as trades. He'd cheat Belzebub himself.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: The man who sold me the spectacles, for a hundred.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But he was a scholar—well read in the Cosmogony.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! He had thee there, Doctor—he had thee there. I know 'un. Sink me—Jonathan, and Merrythoughts, and Brosus! It's the one bit of book-learning he has got to his back, and he always brings it out to take scholars in with. Well, they do say scholars he woundy easy to take in, Doctor—but I am zorry he hath nicked thee! Good night, all—good night. But I'll hang the rascal yet.

div.stage: (Exit Farmer L. D. F.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Dr. Primrose!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Deborah!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Father!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Moses!—my children!—we have been all cozened together. Let the misfortunes of the day teach us humility.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Our two horses gone, and nothing to show for them but these nasty green spectacles. Oh, I hate the sight of them!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, Deborah, to grieve over the past is multiplying sorrow by two. Livy shall sing us some merry ditty or other. Where can the little minx be lingering?

div.stage: Enter Dick in great consternation. (L. D. F.)

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Oh, papa! Oh, mother! Oh, the man—the man!

sp.speaker: Dr. P. | Mrs. P.
sp.p: What is it? What's the matter, child?

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Oh! the man told me that sister Livy's gone—gone away.

sp.speaker: Dr. P. | Mrs. P.
sp.p: Livy!—gone ?—gone ?

div.stage: [Moses runs to door L. and looks out.

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: She has ridden away with a gentleman in a post-chaise.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But who?—who?

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: The man said Mr. Burchell.

div.stage: [Dr. P. staggers back, assisted by Mrs. P. and Moses, to arm-chair.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Moses—Moses—look to your father!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p:
Oh, may Heaven's everlasting fury light on him and his! To rob me of the child I was leading up to heaven!
But go, wife!—go, children!—go!—all is over!—my heart is broken within me!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Father—father! is this your fortitude?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Fortitude?—yes, he shall see I have fortitude. Boy, reach me my pistols! I'll follow him all over the world! Old as I am, he shall find I can sting him yet, the villain! (Sinks into chair.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Husband! dearest husband!—Here (pointing to the Bible) is the only weapon fit for thy old hands now. Patience—patience!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Sir, your rage is too violent—villain as he is, you should not have cursed him.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Did I curse him, boy?—did I?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Indeed, Sir, you did.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Then may Heaven forgive me and him! But my child !—to undo my child—the light of my eyes—my treasure! Had she but died!—but she is dishonoured! Oh! may a curse—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P., Sophy, and Moses
sp.p: Father!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Heaven forgive me! what was I going to say? Poor thing!—poor thing!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: We shall never call her daughter more! She may bring us to shame, but she shall never darken these doors again!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Woman—woman! I will go forth and find her. If I may not save her from shame, I may bring back a lost lamb to the fold of a father's heart—where she shall be welcome, were she ten thousand times a sinner!—Boy, give me my hat and staff.

div.stage: [Music.—Moses gives him hat and stick from table L.H. Curtain slowly descends on group.)
(Bill. . Dick.
Sophia. Mrs. P. Dr. P. Moses.)

div.head: Scene I
div.stage: Slow Music.—A mean room in a Village Alehouse.—A table R. H., and arm chair L. of table.—Symonds the Landlord, and Dr. Primrose.—A bottle and glass on table.

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, another glass will hearten you up after your fever. Your reverence had very nigh given the doctors the slip.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: A fortnight here, and not strength to travel yet; but I will start to-day, if I die. I must find her.

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: Your reverence will not be strong enough to leave the Harrow for this month—(aside) when we do get a good customer, it's the least we can do to keep him.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, it's not the body, Master Symonds (puts his hand to his breast), 'tis here I suffer. I must start to day. I must find her, if I die.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Symonds, L. D. flat.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Mr. Symonds, you use me very ill, and I'll bear it no longer. Here's three parts of the business left for me to do, and the fourth left undone, while you do nothing but soak with the guests all day long; whereby, if a spoonful of liquor were to cure me of a fever, I never touch a drop.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, dame, you must not be angry. Take a glass to my health, and your husband's.

div.stage: [Pours one out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Sir, your health (drinks). 'Tis not the value of the liquor, I mind, but one must fret when the house is going out of the windows. If there's a customer to be dunned, 'tis I am called in. He'd as lief eat that glass as budge himself.

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: Mrs. S., Mrs. S., remember you're the weaker vessel, and should put up with the disagreeables.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: There, now, we've a young woman lodging up stairs, and I don't believe she's got a rap, by her over civility. She's mighty slow of asking for her bill.

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: Never mind, if she's slow, she's sure.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Sure, quotha! There's one thing sure, that she's been here close on a fortnight, and we've never seen the cross of her money.

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: Consider, wife, she's a gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Gentle or simple, she pays to-day, or out she shall pack, with a sassarara. Gentry may be fine things, where they take; but for my part, I never saw much good of them at the sign of the Harrow.

div.stage: Exit Mrs. Symonds L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Poor creature! Alas, for the helplessness that falls into the hands of thy better half, Mr. Symonds.

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: Ah, women will be women, your reverence, but Mrs. Symonds' is a strong case.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Out, I say, hussey! tramp this moment, or I'll mark thee for a three months. Out, I say.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Symonds, driving in Olivia. L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh! dear madam, pity me, a poor abandoned creature; but for one night, and death will soon do the rest.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Stand off there, fiend. (Seizing Olivia in his arms.) My child !—my—

div.stage: [Choked with his emotions.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh! my own, dear—

sp.speaker: Sym.
sp.p: We are not wanted here, wife; come. This comes of not knowing a gentlewoman.

div.stage: Exeunt Symonds and Mrs. S. L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Welcome! any way welcome; my dearest lost one, my treasure, to your poor old father's bosom. Though the vicious forsake thee, there is one in the world that will never forsake thee; though thou hast ten thousand crimes to answer, he will forgive them all.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh, my dearest, best, papa! I do not deserve this. You cannot forgive me—I know you cannot.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I do—I do—from my heart—only repent, and we shall see many happy days yet.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Never, never, my life, henceforth, must be infamy abroad, and shame at home. (Faintly.) I shall die.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Thou shalt not die my lamb. (Leads her to table R.) No, no. Drink—drink. (Gives her wine.)

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: But you look so thin and pale, papa. It was not for me, papa? You did not grieve over your poor Livy. You are too good—too wise.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Too wise, young woman. (Sternly.)

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh! no, no, papa; you never called me by so cold a name before.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Forgive me, darling; but we are fools the wisest of us, and bad the best. But how cam'st thou here, dear, and in this sad plight?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Oh! I will tell you all—all. That villain from the first day he professed love for me, made me honourable though private proposals.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Villain, indeed—who would have thought that a man of Mr. Burchell's seeming good sense and honesty could step into our family to undo it.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Mr. Burchell! Nay, papa, he was ever my friend, and warned me often against the arts of him I loved too well—alas !-of Mr. Thornhill.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Thornhill!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Yes, it was he seduced me from you under promise of marriage. I loved him then, and believed him. The ceremony was performed—for a while he was kind. I urged him to come back to you, with me; or to send me back and acknowledge our marriage; weary at last of my prayers and tears, he told me the shameful truth, that license and priest were false, and that I was his mistress and not his wife.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Heaven pardon him and comfort thee.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: I think I was mad for some days after that. But so soon as I was myself again, I fled from him, I so longed father, to creep back near you all—not home, father—I durst not come home; but thought if I could get to the village perhaps, and die there, I should die happier.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Thou shalt not die, my own lamb—thou shalt come home with me, and their hearts will leap for joy at the poor prodigal's return, as mine doth now.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: It is too much joy—father—dear father, I feel so faint—so happy.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Come, darling, thou shalt lie down awhile, and I will watch thee (leading her in.)

div.stage: Music.—Exit L. D. F.

div.head: Scene II.
div.stage: Interior of the Vicar's Cottage.—Table R.—Arm-chair R. of fire-place, chair R. of table, and chair L. of table.—Small table L., with guitar and needlework on it, and chair L.—Mrs. Primrose, Moses, Sophia.—Music.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Sophy, child, shut the door—(L. of table. Sophia goes out L. and returns.)—'Tis very cold—and I'm so nervous, and low, and wretched, in thy father's absence, that I have no natural warmth in me. Moses, what dost thou mean by always poring over thy books, instead of comforting thy mother?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: 'Tis Epictetus, mother—a book that teaches patience under misfortunes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Drat the boy! Thou dost not see thy mother learning patience out of books. But I've none to comfort me since our Livy—since thy sister left us.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Why make our regret bitterer by always harping on it?

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: You judge her too severely, mamma.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Judge?—you cannot judge a mother's feelings; and now thy father's left us, too, a fortnight, and no news of him.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Perhaps he has been ill, mother.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Why, thou unnatural child, dost thou wish to frighten me to death? How canst thou be so cruel, Sophy? (A knock at door L.) Some of the neighbours, I dare say; but they sha'n't see us downhearted (dries her eyes and rises)—we will shew a spirit, child, as becomes the Primroses. Open the door.

div.stage: Enter Clink and Bailiff L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Is Parson Primrose within, an't please you?

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: My father is not at home—he has been absent for these three weeks. Did you want him?

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Hum! yes—that is, the law wants him, young man.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And here's the law come upon us, as if we hadn't misery enough already!

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: We've a writ against him.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: A writ against my father!—at whose suit?

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Squire Thornhill's, for forty pounds.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: The Squire? Squire Thornhill, who wanted to marry into the family—the best friend we have in the world? Why, he lent him the money to pay his printer's bill!

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: And now he wants it back again. The best of friends must be paid, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Why, all we have in the house isn't worth the money; but we are honest, Sir, and proud, though we are poor—take it all, and we'll live like Robinson Crusoe on a desolate island.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: I'm afeard you won't have much left in the house when the law has had its share.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: The law again, man? Isn't the law satisfied with taking all we have in the world?

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: The law's never satisfied, ma'am. We've a distress warrant for the rent due at Michaelmas to Squire Thornhill.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Squire Thornhill again—and distraining for his rent? Oh! if ever there was a serpent in a red coat and laced hat, 'tis this Squire Thornhill!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: The unfeeling scoundrel!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: But there must be some mistake.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: The law never makes mistakes, ma'am; or if it do, it never owns 'em—and 'tis all one. Take your inventory, Jonathan—the Squire must be paid.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: He is a hard-hearted scoundrel!—tell him so from me; and if I had him here, I'd thrash him as soundly with my fists as I ever did with my arguments!

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Cheer up, dear mamma!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And just now, when your wicked sister has left us, and your father has gone in search of her, and we have had no news of him for a fortnight—Oh! it's too much—too much!

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: We must seize the sticks, ma'am, now we've taken the inventory. (Going to small table L.)

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Touch a chair or a table, and I'll annihilate you!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh! Moses—Moses! if you go and get yourself hanged, I shall have nobody to protect me!

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Be calm, dear brother.

div.stage: [Crosses to Moses, and clinging to him.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Come, be reasonable, young man—we're two to one, without counting the majesty of the law.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Stand back, I say.

div.stage: Enter Vicar L. D. F.—He appears pale and enfeebled by long sickness.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: What means this?

div.stage: [Moses gets round to R.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: My husband! How thin and pale thou art.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Dear, papa.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Father !

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I have been ill, but I am strong again, my loves. And now explain, what is going on here? Who are these men? Why do I find thee in tears? And why this passion, boy?

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: You're our prisoner (tapping him on shoulder), begging your reverence's pardon, at the suit of Edward Thornhill, Esq., for forty pounds. And here's a distress warrant for the half year's rent, due to the Squire at Michaelmas.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: You know me friends, and can trust my word; leave us together for a few minutes, I promise you not to attempt escape.

div.stage: Exit Clink and Bailiff, touching their hats respectfully L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, Charles, Charles, this is a sorry return for thee. And thou hast been ill, my poor husband, and among strangers—not in thy home—home, alas, alas! it is no home now, for she we loved most of all, is gone; there stands her empty chair, and her work, and her guitar, as she left it. What does it do here, reminding us of her? (Going to remove them.) No, no, I cannot—I have not the heart to touch them—for I loved her—oh ! how I loved her!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, my love, let us acknowledge the goodness that blesses with one hand, while it chastens with the other. What is all we lose here—what is a prison compared to the comfort I bring with me? Our lost lamb is found—our Olivia is come back.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Come back! my Livy! my darling! But no—this may be the scene of ruin; but still it is the abode of innocence—we know no daughter Olivia, now.

div.stage: [Sinks into chair L. of table.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Woman, woman! What mercy can they look for, that show none? For shame—hearken to the mother's heart that is working in thee even now, and not to the devil of pride that plucks it down.

div.stage: [He goes to the door, and returns bringing in Olivia.—Tableau.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Livy, dear sister! Forgive her, mother.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Forgive her, mother.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: So madam, this is but a poor place you are returned to. Look around you, girl, you left a happy home—a home of comfort, and love, and happiness. You come back to a scene of ruin, of sadness, and shame, and broken hearts—'tis your making. Yes, your poor father and I have suffered very much of late; but I hope Heaven will forgive you.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p:
Oh! mother, mother, if you but knew all I have suffered. How, from the day I left you, lured by the falsehoods of a villain, your grief has been in my thoughts by day and my dreams by night. How I have prayed and prayed for strength to return and ask forgiveness—forgiveness for your poor Livy, that you loved so, and made so much of, and who has been so wretched. Oh! if you knew all, you would not—you would not look so cold,
and proud, and stern upon me—you could not dear, kind, mother—you could not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh! Livy! Livy! my poor, lost girl, how wan and wasted thou art, child—and thy poor eyes heavy and red with crying; and there is the locket still round thy neck, that I hung there when thou wert an innocent babe in thy cradle—and now—I forgive thee. Bless thee, poor child! bless thee!

div.stage: [Rises and brings her down.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And now let the worst come—strong in our love and faith—we will meet it with resignation— Enter Thornhill, L. D. F.—comes down L.) Oh, villain!

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: Curse him!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Do not lift thy hand, boy. See there, your victim, Sir. Do you come to gloat over the misery you have made?

div.stage: [Thornhill approaches.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Stand back! I am her mother. Think of your own, and respect her grey hairs in mine. Leave this house. You did your worst when you brought her to shame. What terrors has a prison for broken hearts like ours?

sp.speaker: Thornhill.
sp.p: I told her what would come of leaving me; but it is not yet too late. I love her still, let her return to me and you are a free man.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Age has cooled my passions, and my calling restrains them—I loathe and scorn you!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: So, you reject my offer, the worst has not yet come upon you. We shall soon see which is the fittest object for scorn; you or I.

div.stage: Re-enter Bailiff and Clink, L. D. F.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: My friends this is severe weather to take me to prison. I am not yet well recovered of a fever, and I am too weak and old to walk far through the snow. But, if it must be so, get together the little that is ours, my love (to Mrs. P.) and let us quit this place. You will come with me?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: My work—my work.

div.stage: ([She falls into a swoon.])

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Look to your poor sister, Sophy; let her but come to herself, and then, Sirs, we are ready.

div.stage: [The door is suddenly burst open violently, and the Villagers enter, headed by Flamborough.

sp.speaker: Flam.
sp.p: Where are the rogues that would take our good pastor from us. Seize them, lads—duck 'em—hang 'em. Sheep-faced rascals.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: What, my friends, is this the way you love me ? Is this what I have taught you, to fly in the face of justice—to bring ruin on yourselves and me? Alas! my dear friends, return to the duty you owe to your God, your country, and to me. Go, go. Good bye—good bye.

div.stage: [Music—Flamborough and Villagers crowd round him, kissing his hand.
Scene Closes.

div.head: Scene III.—An outer Ward in a Prison.
div.stage: Enter Ephraim Jenkinson, with fetters on (humming a song).

sp.l: Then I goes up Holborn-hill,
In a cart,
At St. Giles's drinks my fill,
And at Tyburn makes my will—
sp.p: —Caged at last—and with Flamborough's indictment for forgery against me at the next Assizes. Yes, 'tis the nab cheat this time. No more cantering across commons for Ephraim Jenkinson! The only horse I shall ever ride again will be the colt foaled of an acorn, and he is ridden in a halter—But hang care; our host here keeps a mighty pretty Nantz. So, ho! Clink, my boy! (Enter Clink L. H.) —A pint of brandy, d'ye hear, burnt, a clean pipe with Virginia, and the Bow-street Gazetteer—I want to study the last fashions for Tyburn.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Nay, you must wait, Captain—here's fresh company come, and we have to get their rooms ready—'tis a clergyman, and I know what is due to the cloth—ask our chaplain else, he hath ever the longest score in the prison tap-room.

div.stage: [Loud laughing L. H.
Enter Dr. Primrose L.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: The old parson, by all that's unsophisticated!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: What a scene! Instead of weeping, and wailing, and repentance—riot, and laughter, and profanity !—a hell upon earth!

div.stage: Enter Prisoners L. H.

sp.speaker: Pris.
sp.p: Garnish!—garnish!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Eh?

sp.speaker: 1st Pris.
sp.p: Twig the parson!

sp.speaker: 2nd Pris.
sp.p: Smoke his reverence!

div.stage: (advancing towards him)

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Stand back, you queer cuffins, or I'll put some of your glims into mourning! This gentry cove is a friend of mine. (To Dr. P.) Give them what small money you may have about you. (Dr. P. gives it.) And now be off to your house, and leave gentlemen to themselves!

sp.speaker: 1st Pris.
sp.p: Here, Clink, a gallon of rum bouse, into the parlour—and pipes for the party, you rogue!

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Ay, ay, gentlemen!

div.stage: Exeunt Clink and Prisoners L. H.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Have you provided yourself with a bed, Sir?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, I knew not—

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p:
That's unfortunate, for they allow nothing but straw—and 'tis cold lying on the flags at this time of year. But
you're a gentleman, and so am I—so, between gentlemen, half my bed is at your service.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Sir, you are very kind—sweet is company in affliction ! If we are alone, the world is but a prison.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: The world, Sir?—the world, Sir, is in its dotage. The cosmogony or creation of the world has puzzled philosophers—Sanconiathon, Manetho—

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Eh?—why, surely I have heard those opinions before! Had I not once the pleasure of seeing you at Welbridge Fair?—and is not your name Ephraim Jenkinson? I sold you a horse there.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Yes, and I remember I forgot to pay for him. And there was that draft on your neighbour Flamborough. Curse my taste for letters! He intends to swear against me for a forger, at the next Assizes, before the harman beak—the judge, Sir, I mean—and then—(imitates the action of hanging.)

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Nay, your kindness in offering to assist me shall be rewarded. I think I can soften or suppress Flamborough's evidence, and you need not fear me; but one thing you must promise.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Sir, I am a man of my word—I promise anything.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Repent of your past sins, and leave this life for an honester.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: 'Tis easy said, Sir; but who will give me the chance? No, I've the gaol brand upon me, and must carry it to the gallows, I fear—but I'll do my best.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Surely, with your ingenuity—

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Ah, Sir, had I but bestowed half the pains in learning a trade, that I have in learning to be a scoundrel, I might have been a rich man at this day; but rogue as I am, I may be your friend when you least expect it. Heaven bless and prosper you, Sir.

div.stage: [Retires up c.
Re-enter Clink, L. H.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: This way, old gentleman, we must put you in the common ward for the present. 'Tis a little rough at first; but you'll soon get used to it.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I may have my wife and children with me?

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Why, it's against the rules; but one might do it (holding out his hand) out of humanity—Sir—only out of humanity.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.stage: (Coming forward c., gives him money, unperceived by Doctor.)
sp.p: There—

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: I'll show 'em into you, Sir, directly.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: I thank thee, friend—thou art too good for this trade.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, one has one's feelings, like another.

div.stage: Exit Clink and Dr. Primrose. L. H.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p:
Yes, if I could find the gentleman with the crabstick, who broke my head, when the Squire carried off his
daughter. The girl has left him, I know, and if I could but prove it, I should live for the future on better terms with myself.

div.head: Scene IV.
div.stage: The common Ward of the Prison.—c. door.—On the right, seated on a Bench, are Dr. P. Mrs. P., Olivia, Sophia, Dick and Bill.—On the left are Prisoners beating hemp on blocks, and some playing on the ground.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: And, now, away with these blocks, till after dinner. we expect company, and I'd have the ward tidy. Come, bustle, or I'll smarten some of you with my rattan; and see that you hide your brandy bottles. I'll shew them a well-ordered prison, I warrant.
sp.stage: [They carry the blocks off L.—Exit L.

div.stage: Exit Clink, C. D.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: And how dost thou feel now, my poor love?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: The damp of these walls chills me to the bone. But cold, and wet, and hunger, are nothing to the wretchedness and wickedness round about us. Still, cheer up, my little ones. We should have light hearts, for our consciences are clear.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Not mine, not mine.

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: I wish I was big enough to fight the wicked man that put you in this nasty plce—I'd like to kill him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: What—and is this the way thou rememberest thy father's lesson. What should we do to our enemies, sirrah?

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Thresh 'em.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah, nature is stronger than preaching, in the little wretches; but my heart migives me about Moses.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Not so mine—he is a good, brave boy—and come what will, he will do his duty. Perhaps he is seeking succour for us.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, that abominable Squire! and how you have wronged poor Mr. Burchell—

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: I told you so, mamma—for my heart assured me he was honest from the first.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, I ever said so.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: This way with the murdering villain— and see that he hath the forty pound irons—a blood-thirsty ruffian!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Oh, pray, Mr. Gaoler, do not bring any murdering villain, or blood thirsty ruffian here.

div.stage: [They get up and come forward.
Clink enters C. D.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Them as can't afford private apartments, ma'am. must take up with such company as we chooses, saving your presence.

div.stage: Enter Turnkeys dragging in Moses bleeding, and in irons, C. D.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Moses!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: My boy!

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Brother!

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Dear brother!

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: My boy! bleeding! oh, thou art hurt! And in fetters! Oh, why is this, Sir? ((To Clink).) He is innocent —I am his mother—I tell you he is innocent.

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Innocent, quotha! A bloodthirsty highwavman!

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: What hast thou done, unhappy boy?

sp.speaker: Clink.
sp.p: Done? Why he stopped and nearly murdered a gentleman on the King's highway, a rascally footpad, as he is. Done, indeed! But, I'll go and have our Little Ease got ready for him. 'Tis ancle deep in snow, and his hot spirit needs a cooling

div.stage: Exit Clink and Turnkeys, C. D.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: A robber—my boy a robber? Speak, and say it is not true.

sp.speaker: Moses.
sp.p: It is a lie, Sir. Almost mad with grief and rage at the misery that this villain has brought upon my poor sister, and his cruelty to you, Sir, I followed him. I scarcely knew what I meant to do. I had no weapon. I came up with him, and told him the truth—that he was a coward, a liar, and a villain. He drew upon me. I wrested his sword from his hand, and broke it. We were both wounded in the scuffle, and his people, by his desire, seized me, and brought me hither, on a charge of having attempted to rob their master.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah! my poor Moses!

div.stage: [Moses turns up and crosses to R.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But this was wanted to fill the cup of our sorrows, The wicked shall not always triumph.

div.stage: Enter Jenkinson, L, H.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Your servant, ladies, I have spoken with honest Clink, Doctor, for a more suitable room for you and your family. These children are too handsome and too good for a place like this.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Bless them all! you are very kind.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: I see one here that I have injured, in my late way of business, and by whom I wish to be forgiven.

div.stage: [Offering his hand to Moses.

sp.speaker: Moses
sp.p: Nay, I protest, I never saw you before, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: You remember a certain gross of green spectacles.

div.stage: [Moses turns up, and comes down L.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: It was a vile trick to play on an innocent lad.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: It was his white stockings and the black ribbon in his hair, that were fatal to him. I may say, for your comfort, Sir, that I never, in a long experience of the greener sort—for I have been quite a pigeon fancier—saw an honester face, or a simpler. But how came you by that broken pate. and these darbies? Oh! Egad, they do you honour, Sir. They put you ten pounds above me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah! we may thank Squire Thornhill for this.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Oh! if the law would but let me loose a little to do justice, I'd gibbet Ned Thornhill to scorn, like a kite on a barn-gable.

div.stage: Enter Clink shewing in Burchell, C. D.

sp.speaker: Sophia.
sp.p: Burchell!

sp.speaker: Dick.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Burchell.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: My dear friends, this is a sad sight; but how—

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Ah, you may well say "How?" Mr. Burchell. How indeed, but by the arts of a villain—that Squire Thornhill, who, not satisfied with undoing the daughter, must throw the father into this horrid prison, and accuse this dear inoffensive lad here of highway robbery, that never had courage to fire off our old blunderbuss at the sparrows!

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Remove those irons—(to Clink L.) Poor boy! poor boy!

div.stage: [Clink takes Moses off L. H.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: But we owe you a reparation, Mr. Burchell; we have injured you by our suspicions—forgive us all!

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: What! Sophia too? But all that is over now. I bring you comfort. Cheer up, my sweet Olivia!—heartless as your husband is—

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Husband? Alas! Sir, do not mock me!

div.stage: Enter Thornhill C. D.—Advancing, he recognises his Uncle.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Ha, my dear Sir! what lucky chance brings you here?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: No fawning, Sir! The way to my heart is by the road of honour. I have watched your conduct, Sir, and find in it but falsehood, cowardice, and oppression.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Another than yourself, Sir, would not dare to use this language.

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Some reparation you may yet make. (Taking Olivia by the hand.) Do you acknowledge this much-injured lady for your wife?

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: There has been no binding ceremony between us. I love her, and will take her to my heart—but my wife she is not.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.stage: (Coming forward L. C, lays his hand on Thornhill's shoulder.)
sp.p: That's a lie! saving your presence, Doctor.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Ha! Jenkinson?

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Yes, Jenkinson! who is about quitting the devil's service, in which his wages for some time past have been—a mouthful of oaths, an empty belly, and a promissory note for the gallows. Here stands Ephraim Jenkinson, who, rogue as he is, dares to look without blushing in the face of Ned Thornhill!

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p:
This fellow comes just in time to convince you and all here that the license was a forgery, and the priest a
suborned sot of his own kidney, and no true clergyman. Nay, do not think that I glory in this now. Since she left me, and this good man was brought hither by my means, I have had no peace. I admit my villany, and I deplore it.

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Comfort yourself as to that, Squire—'twas a true license and a true priest, or the sorrel mare dropped for it.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Neither the world nor the law will take this rogue's word for it—and what other witness is there?

sp.speaker: Burch.
sp.p: Sir William Thornhill, Sir.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Sir William Thornhill!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Burchell no longer; but Sir William Thornhill, your friend. Yes, Sir, informed of your design by one of your own instruments, I reached your place of meeting too late to rescue this lady from your hands; but not too late to overpower your agent here—

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Then the crab-stick cudgel?—

div.stage: [Feels his head and retires up.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: —(Holding it up) To outstrip you at the Moat-house and, by his information, to substitute a genuine license, and a true priest for the false ones. This lady, Sir, is your wife in the eye of the law, as in honour and in conscience.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Come to my arms,—my child—my darling —thou wilt be a credit to thy family yet, as I ever said thou wouldst.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Sir, you have foiled me at my own weapons. Perhaps you will hardly credit my assurance now, that I came here to undo part of the misery I had caused, by releasing Dr. Primrose and his son from this place; to which, in my first flush of anger at Olivia's flight, I had consigned them. As for Olivia here, my wife, I dare not ask her to return to me.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: We will give you time, Sir, to test the sincerity of your repentance. I will continue to you, Sir, one sixth of the allowance you now receive of me, on condition that you leave this lady unmolested, till she choose to recall you to her affections.

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.p: Much as you have wronged me, my heart still pleads for you; but my better judgment tells me that after so long a course of cruelty and deceit, you should be tested by something more than the hasty repentance of a moment. If the end of a year should find you, indeed, changed in your habits, you will find Olivia still unchanged in her love.

sp.speaker: Thorn.
sp.p: Your sentence is just, and if I may indeed hope by the efforts of a year, to blot out the crimes and follies of a life, I shall return to you changed in all things, dear Olivia, but my affection for thee.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: He promises well, and I think we may trust him. But. where is this honest rogue, who has set the fashion of repentance? Come, thou hast done enough of good to day to make up for all thy sins in the way of robbing and cozening,

sp.speaker: Jen.
sp.p: Indeed, Sir William, I would fain hope so; your kindness gives me pride in my new trade of honesty—to say nothing of a certain easiness about the throat, which I have long been a stranger to. And I trust this deed will be a little item on the creditors' side, to set off against the heavy per contra of Ephraim Jenkinson's last account.

div.stage: Bows, and exit, L. H. 1 E.
Re-enter Moses, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: And now, my good friends—here is a dear girl for whom we must find a husband—what say you, Mrs. Primrose?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: Nay, Sir William, nobody takes my advice, so I'll offer none. But if I were to make a choice, methinks I know where the child's inclinations point.

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: And said I not truly, my love, that the wicked would not always prosper?

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.p: True, my dear, and have I not always supported thee in thy becoming sentiments?

sp.speaker: Dr. P.
sp.p: Time will heal thy wounds, my darling, and then I have nothing this side of the grave to wish for. And may all those who suffer, when they feel disposed to repine at their lot, draw consolation from the source where we have found it.

div.stage: [Crosses to c.

sp.speaker: Vicar
sp.l: Thus, with his children, spare a father's pride,
And her, his old companion, by his side.
Friend of the young, and cherish'd by the old,
"Wakefield's poor Vicar on the scene behold.
To venture here, he quits dear Goldsmith's page—
Must he go back, or may he keep the stage ?

sp.speaker: Olivia.
sp.l: Let poor Olivia, who your hearts, erewhile,
Hath tried to wring, now crave one little smile.
Wife, and no wife, give me time for relenting,
And my sad Squire a few nights for repenting.

sp.speaker: Mrs. P.
sp.l: Take my advice for once, in rhyme and reason;
I may advise, I hope, and yet no treasen ?
Poor Deborah's counsels sure should be worth prizing;
Remember! 'tis her last year of advising.
'Tis fitting she should linger latest here,
With this old friend and faithful helpmate near.
Yes, hand in hand, through triumphs and through trials,
We've hail'd your plaudits, bow'd to your denials.
For the brief season that I here delay,
Let your old servant plead for this new Play!

div.stage: (Sophia, Burchell, Dick, Olivia, Dr. P., Mrs. P., Bill, Moses.)
(R. H. Curtain. L. H.)

body.trailer: Munro, Printer, Queen's Head Yard, Gt. Queen St.
